There is also a conceptual gap between the rigor established for insulating solids and the treatment of electrochemical interfaces.
AI.method: The authors introduce the screened electrochemical Born effective charge (SEBEC), defined as a mixed total-energy derivative that measures the force response of an atomic degree of freedom to interfacial charging under electrochemical boundary conditions.
AI.result: SEBECs provide an unambiguous decomposition of global response and yield the same formal structures for structural relaxation, capacitance, and electrochemical Stark tuning that are familiar from solid-state response theory.
AI.conclusion: The broader implication is a local response framework that brings electrochemical interfaces closer to the conceptual rigor long established for insulating solids, with SEBECs playing a role in electrochemistry analogous to that of Born effective charges in the modern theory of polarization.

title: Two Strategies to Measure Spin-Orbit-Torque Efficiency Acting on the Insulating Magnet Li$_{0.5}$Al$_{0.7}$Fe$_{1.8}$O$_4$
summary: For insulating magnets, widely-used electrically-based techniques to measure spin-orbit-torque efficiency can suffer from poor signal-to-noise ratios and unwanted artifacts, while optical measurements based on conventional magneto-optical Kerr effect (MOKE) imaging often lack sufficient sensitivity. Here we analyze two strategies for measuring the spin-torque efficiency acting on an insulating magnet, focusing on the torque from Pt acting on thin films of the low-damping magnet lithium aluminum ferrite (LAFO). First, lateral + longitudinal spin-torque ferromagnetic resonance (ST-FMR) allows separation of the spin-torque signal from artifacts due to spin-pumping and resonant heating. With this technique, we measure a spin-torque efficiency $ξ^\text{ST-FMR}_\text{DL}\sim\ 0.07$, comparable to but a bit less than for Pt acting on metallic ferromagnets. Second, we attempted optical measurements of spin-orbit-torque-induced magnetic deflection using Sagnac interferometry. We find that Sagnac interferometry provides sufficient sensitivity to measure signals from 14.4 nm LAFO thin films, but the inferred torque efficiency is much weaker than the result from lateral + longitudinal ST-FMR. We speculate that there may be another contribution to the Sagnac signal other than current-induced magnetic deflection, perhaps an out-of-plane component of itinerant electron spins. This becomes relevant for insulating magnets in which the magneto-optic coupling coefficient is very weak.

AI.tldr: Two strategies are compared to measure spin-orbit-torque efficiency in the insulating magnet LAFO/Pt: lateral + longitudinal ST-FMR gives ξ ≈ 0.07, while Sagnac interferometry, though sensitive enough for 14.4 nm films, yields a much weaker apparent efficiency, suggesting a non-magnetic artifact.
AI.motivation: Electrical spin-orbit-torque measurements on insulating magnets suffer from poor signal-to-noise and artifacts, and conventional MOKE imaging often lacks sensitivity. Reliable quantification of spin-torque efficiency in low-damping insulating ferrimagnets is therefore needed.
AI.method: Lateral + longitudinal spin-torque ferromagnetic resonance (ST-FMR) is used to separate the spin-torque signal from spin-pumping and resonant-heating artifacts for Pt on thin LAFO films. Sagnac interferometry is also applied to optically detect spin-orbit-torque-induced magnetic deflection in 14.4 nm LAFO films.
AI.result: ST-FMR yields a damping-like spin-torque efficiency ξ_DL ≈ 0.07, comparable to but slightly lower than Pt on metallic ferromagnets. Sagnac interferometry is sensitive enough to detect signals from 14.4 nm LAFO films, but the inferred torque efficiency is much weaker than the ST-FMR value.
AI.conclusion: Lateral + longitudinal ST-FMR is the more reliable method for insulating magnets. The discrepancy with Sagnac results suggests an additional contribution to the Sagnac signal, possibly an out-of-plane component of itinerant electron spins, which is relevant when magneto-optic coupling is weak.

title: Observation of complex orbital order in MnV2O4
comment: 7 pages, 4 figures, supplementary text with 7 supplementary figures and 7 supplementary tables
summary: Orbital ordering in vanadium spinel oxides with a geometrically frustrated pyrochlore structure has been a subject of controversy, owing to competing theoretical models and the absence of direct experimental evidence. Here we combine high-precision single-crystal synchrotron x-ray diffraction with core differential fourier synthesis to visualize the valence electron density (VED) of the orbital-ordered ground state in real space. By carefully investigating multiple-scattering artifacts, we identify the low-temperature structure as belonging to the I41/amd space group. The reconstructed VED around the V sites reveals an orbital-ordered state distinct from both previously proposed real- and complex-orbital models. Our results resolve the long-standing controversy in MnV2O4 and establish a route to identifying orbital states in frustrated spin-orbital systems.

AI.tldr: By combining single-crystal synchrotron x-ray diffraction with core differential Fourier synthesis, the authors visualize the valence electron density in the orbital-ordered ground state of MnV2O4, identifying an I41/amd symmetry and a novel orbital-ordered state that resolves a long-standing controversy.
AI.motivation: Orbital ordering in vanadium spinel oxides with a geometrically frustrated pyrochlore lattice has long been controversial, driven by competing theoretical models and a lack of direct experimental evidence.
AI.method: High-precision single-crystal synchrotron x-ray diffraction combined with core differential Fourier synthesis to reconstruct the valence electron density (VED) in real space, with careful treatment of multiple-scattering artifacts.
AI.result: The low-temperature structure is identified as I41/amd, and the reconstructed VED reveals an orbital-ordered state distinct from both previously proposed real- and complex-orbital models.
AI.conclusion: The work resolves the long-standing controversy in MnV2O4 and establishes a route to identifying orbital states in frustrated spin-orbital systems.

title: Charge order before superconductivity in the doped kagome Dirac spin liquid
summary: Doping a quantum spin liquid is expected to give a superconductor. On kagome it gives charge order first, because of band structure rather than interaction. In the chargon (Higgs) construction of its U(1) Dirac spin liquid the two gauge components, degenerate on square and triangular lattices, are split by a line-graph effect: one disperses, four minima at $-(1+\sqrt6)t$; the other has two exactly flat lowest bands at $-2t$. Only the dispersive component condenses, over a bare-mass window of width exactly $(\sqrt6-1)t$, in which the doped spin liquid forms charge and loop-current crystals on the $M$, $K$ and $K/2$ stars, the physical U(1) unbroken: a chargon Higgs phase that does not superconduct. Its pairing channels are those of the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ descendants, a pair-density wave, uniform $d+id$ excluded at leading order and at all orders on the $M$ star. The projective symmetry group reduces the quartic competition to one angle, on which projected on-site repulsion sits exactly at the $M$/$K/2$ boundary, a direction protected to all orders by $O(4)\times U(1)$ under renormalization, though lattice matching gives the physical coupling off-ray components. The competing $M$-star crystals are degenerate through sextic order, split only at eighth. The charge sector carries its own classification, the charged counterpart of the undoped bilinear-and-monopole catalog, which holds no charge-carrying operator; it puts the doped Mott insulator and kagome metals on one $F$-irrep grid, separated by the charge-order irrep ($F_1$ there, $F_3$ here) and the Landau cubic. Predicted: $C_2$-odd ($F_3$) charge order, no cubic invariant; vestigial pair phases of period $h/4e$ or $h/6e$; loop-current fields of order ten gauss at herbertsmithite's $^{17}$O and $^{35}$Cl; and, if the $Γ$ flux orders with the condensate, charge and current order setting in together below the condensation scale.

AI.tldr: Doping a kagome spin liquid yields charge order rather than superconductivity, driven by band structure. The split chargon components produce a non-superconducting Higgs phase with charge and loop-current crystals, plus a rich set of testable predictions.
AI.motivation: Doping a quantum spin liquid is generally expected to produce a superconductor. On the kagome lattice, however, charge order appears first. This work aims to explain why charge order preempts superconductivity, attributing it to band structure rather than interactions, and to characterize the resulting phases and their experimental signatures.
AI.method: Using the chargon (Higgs) construction of the kagome U(1) Dirac spin liquid, the two gauge components—degenerate on square and triangular lattices—are shown to be split by a line-graph effect: one disperses with four minima at −(1+√6)t, the other has two exactly flat lowest bands at −2t. Only the dispersive component condenses. A projective symmetry group analysis reduces the quartic competition to a single angle, and renormalization plus lattice matching are used to classify the charge sector and the competing crystal orders.
AI.result: Only the dispersive component condenses, within a bare-mass window of width exactly (√6−1)t, forming charge and loop-current crystals on the M, K, and K/2 stars while physical U(1) remains unbroken—a chargon Higgs phase that does not superconduct. Pairing channels are those of the Z2 descendants (a pair-density wave; uniform d+id excluded at leading order and at all orders on the M star). Projected on-site repulsion sits exactly at the M/(K/2) boundary, a direction protected to all orders by O(4)×U(1) under renormalization, though lattice matching gives off-ray components. Competing M-star crystals are degenerate through sextic order, splitting only at eighth order. The charge sector carries its own classification, the charged counterpart of the undoped bilinear-and-monopole catalog, holding no charge-carrying operator, and places the doped Mott insulator and kagome metals on one F-irrep grid separated by the charge-order irrep and the Landau cubic.
AI.conclusion: The work predicts C2-odd (F3) charge order with no cubic invariant; vestigial pair phases of period h/4e or h/6e; loop-current fields of order ten gauss at herbertsmithite's 17O and 35Cl; and, if the Γ flux orders with the condensate, charge and current order setting in together below the condensation scale. It unifies the doped Mott insulator and kagome metals on a single F-irrep grid.

title: Quantum interpretation of classical LiF simulations
summary: Recent studies have shown that classical LiF simulations can reproduce low-temperature experimental spectra when performed at a simulation temperature $T^*$ higher than the physical temperature $T$. We show that the characteristic scale of this rescaling follows naturally from quantum vibrational statistics. An effective temperature $T_{\rm eff}(T)$ is obtained by matching classical and quantum harmonic energies and is evaluated using an analytic acoustic-optical model and a first-principles LiF vibrational density of states $D(\varepsilon)$. The resulting temperature reproduces the low-temperature scale of the reported spectral temperature and approaches the physical temperature in the classical regime. Our results identify zero-point motion and Planck-Bose-Einstein statistics as the origin of the reported temperature scale.

AI.tldr: An effective temperature from matching classical and quantum harmonic energies explains why classical LiF simulations must run at elevated temperatures to reproduce low-temperature spectra, tracing the effect to zero-point motion and Bose-Einstein statistics.
AI.motivation: Classical molecular simulations of LiF only reproduce low-temperature experimental spectra when run at a simulation temperature higher than the physical temperature, and the origin of this temperature rescaling was unexplained. The authors aim to show that the rescaling scale is not empirical but follows from quantum vibrational statistics.
AI.method: The authors define an effective temperature T_eff(T) by matching classical and quantum harmonic energies, then evaluate it using (i) an analytic acoustic-optical model and (ii) a first-principles LiF vibrational density of states D(epsilon).
AI.result: The effective temperature reproduces the low-temperature scale of the reported spectral temperature and converges to the physical temperature in the classical (high-temperature) regime.
AI.conclusion: Zero-point motion and Planck-Bose-Einstein statistics are identified as the origin of the reported temperature scale, providing a physical basis for the simulation-temperature rescaling in classical LiF simulations.

title: Percolation threshold in cluster-assembled nanogranular palladium films and related strategies for hydrogen detection
summary: Electrical transport in cluster-assembled nanogranular palladium films was investigated in-situ during growth by Supersonic Cluster Beam Deposition. The percolation onset is observed at a thickness of 1.5 nm, while the percolation completion at 2.5 nm. Films at the percolation thickness (2 nm) and beyond the percolation end (5 nm) were subsequently exposed ex-situ to 0.25% hydrogen in air to investigate how hydrogen-induced structural changes in Pd clusters modulate electrical transport and can be exploited as mechanism for selective hydrogen detection. Implantation of palladium clusters in soft polymer styrene-ethylene-butylene-styrene was also explored to promote clusters separation and enhance quantum tunnelling phenomena within electrical transport. The observed electrical transport pattern features stable baselines in air, suggesting material stability, fast response time (T50% < 10 s), and the coexistence of reversible and irreversible components in conduction changes induced by hydrogen exposure. The irreversible component is tentatively attributed to hydrogen-promoted partial coalescence of Pd clusters. The behaviour of the polymer implanted samples suggests an alternative gas detection mechanism where hydrogen-induced polymer swelling dominates over palladium structural modifications. These results disclose novel possible transducing routes for miniaturized hydrogen detection and multimodal sensing.

AI.tldr: Electrical transport in cluster-assembled nanogranular Pd films is studied in-situ during SCBD growth, with percolation onset at 1.5 nm and completion at 2.5 nm. Hydrogen exposure of 2 nm and 5 nm films reveals fast, partly reversible conduction changes; polymer-implanted Pd clusters suggest an alternative swelling-based sensing mechanism.
AI.motivation: To understand how hydrogen-induced structural changes in Pd clusters modulate electrical transport, and to exploit this for selective, miniaturized hydrogen detection and multimodal sensing.
AI.method: In-situ electrical transport measurements during Supersonic Cluster Beam Deposition growth of nanogranular Pd films; ex-situ exposure of 2 nm (percolation) and 5 nm (post-percolation) films to 0.25% H2 in air; implantation of Pd clusters in SEBS polymer to promote cluster separation and quantum tunnelling.
AI.result: Percolation onset at 1.5 nm and completion at 2.5 nm. Stable baselines in air, fast response (T50% < 10 s), and coexistence of reversible and irreversible conduction components under hydrogen. Irreversible component tentatively attributed to hydrogen-promoted partial coalescence of Pd clusters; polymer-implanted samples show hydrogen-induced polymer swelling dominating over Pd structural modifications.
AI.conclusion: These findings disclose novel transducing routes for miniaturized hydrogen detection and multimodal sensing.

title: Non-Abelian chiral spin liquid in a spin-$1$ antiferromagnet on the square lattice
summary: Non-Abelian chiral spin liquids (CSLs) host non-Abelian anyon excitations and are promising platforms for topological quantum computation. However, realizing non-Abelian CSLs in short-range interacting spin systems remains elusive. Here, we study a spin-$1$ square-lattice model with the first- and second-neighbor bilinear ($J_1,J_2$) and biquadratic interactions ($K_1,K_2$), as well as the three-spin scalar chiral coupling $J_χ$. Inspired by the evidence of the Moore-Read state in exact diagonalization and infinite Projected Entangled Pair States calculations, we fix $J_1=1.0$, $J_2/J_1=0.623$, $K_1/J_1=-0.176$, and obtain a quantum phase diagram for $0 \leq K_2/J_1 \leq 0.4$ and $0.3 \leq J_χ/J_1 \leq 0.6$ by using the density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) calculations. We identify a stripe antiferromagnetic phase, a Néel antiferromagnetic phase, a magnetically ordered chiral spin state phase, and a non-Abelian CSL phase emerging near the boundaries of the ordered phases. The unbiased DMRG results provide strong evidence for the Moore-Read state, including the three topological sectors, the quantized spin Chern number $C=1$, and the level counting of low-lying entanglement spectra which is consistent with the chiral SU(2)$_2$ conformal field theory. Our results may shed new light on searching for non-Abelian CSLs in other higher-spin ($S > 1/2$) systems with short-range couplings.

AI.tldr: Using DMRG on a spin-1 square-lattice model with bilinear, biquadratic, and chiral three-spin couplings, the authors map a quantum phase diagram and identify a non-Abelian chiral spin liquid consistent with the Moore-Read state.
AI.motivation: Non-Abelian chiral spin liquids host non-Abelian anyons useful for topological quantum computation, but realizing them in short-range interacting spin systems remains elusive. This motivates the search for such a phase in a higher-spin (S=1) model with short-range couplings.
AI.method: The authors study a spin-1 square-lattice model with first- and second-neighbor bilinear (J1, J2) and biquadratic (K1, K2) interactions plus a three-spin scalar chiral coupling Jχ. Guided by exact diagonalization and infinite Projected Entangled Pair States evidence for the Moore-Read state, they fix J1=1.0, J2/J1=0.623, K1/J1=-0.176 and compute the quantum phase diagram for 0 ≤ K2/J1 ≤ 0.4 and 0.3 ≤ Jχ/J1 ≤ 0.6 using density matrix renormalization group (DMRG).
AI.result: DMRG yields four phases: stripe antiferromagnetic, Néel antiferromagnetic, magnetically ordered chiral spin state, and a non-Abelian chiral spin liquid emerging near the boundaries of the ordered phases. The unbiased results provide strong evidence for the Moore-Read state, including three topological sectors, quantized spin Chern number C=1, and low-lying entanglement spectrum level counting consistent with the chiral SU(2)₂ conformal field theory.
AI.conclusion: The results establish a non-Abelian chiral spin liquid (Moore-Read state) in a short-range interacting spin-1 model and may guide the search for non-Abelian CSLs in other higher-spin (S > 1/2) systems with short-range couplings.

title: Unbiased first-principles construction of complete tensorial spin Hamiltonians
comment: 16 pages, 4 figures, supplementary information will be released in publication
summary: Magnetic ground states are commonly predicted using spin Hamiltonians whose interaction terms are selected a priori, potentially overlooking the microscopic interactions that govern complex magnetic order. Here, we introduce a general framework for the unbiased first-principles construction of symmetry-complete tensorial spin Hamiltonians and its automated implementation in AMATIS. The framework constructs the Hamiltonian directly from density-functional theory while rigorously enforcing quantum spin algebra and crystallographic symmetry. Applied to representative two-dimensional van der Waals magnets, the framework reproduces established magnetic interactions and uncovers hidden physics beyond conventional spin models, including chiral interactions that stabilize metastable skyrmions, higher-rank tensorial interactions that reconstruct the magnetic phase diagram and establish stabilizing competing multi-Q phases, and an emergent p-wave altermagnetic electronic structure. Our results demonstrate that unbiased tensorial Hamiltonian construction provides a predictive alternative to the conventional practice of manually selecting spin-model interactions, enabling first-principles discovery of unconventional magnetic phases.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a general framework and its AMATIS implementation for the unbiased, first-principles construction of symmetry-complete tensorial spin Hamiltonians, reproducing known interactions in 2D van der Waals magnets while uncovering hidden physics such as chiral skyrmion-stabilizing interactions, higher-rank tensorial terms, and emergent p-wave altermagnetism.
AI.motivation: Magnetic ground states are typically predicted via spin Hamiltonians with interaction terms chosen a priori, an approach that may overlook microscopic interactions governing complex magnetic order. An unbiased, first-principles alternative is needed.
AI.method: A general framework for constructing symmetry-complete tensorial spin Hamiltonians directly from density-functional theory, rigorously enforcing quantum spin algebra and crystallographic symmetry, with automated implementation in AMATIS.
AI.result: Applied to representative two-dimensional van der Waals magnets, the framework reproduces established magnetic interactions and uncovers hidden physics beyond conventional spin models: chiral interactions stabilizing metastable skyrmions, higher-rank tensorial interactions reconstructing the magnetic phase diagram and establishing stabilizing competing multi-Q phases, and an emergent p-wave altermagnetic electronic structure.
AI.conclusion: Unbiased tensorial Hamiltonian construction offers a predictive alternative to manually selecting spin-model interactions, enabling first-principles discovery of unconventional magnetic phases.

title: Band-Saddle-Point Engineering in Mixed $A$-site $A$V$_3$Sb$_5$ Kagome Metals
summary: $A$V$_3$Sb$_5$ compounds ($A$ = K, Rb, Cs) offer an experimental platform for probing the physics of kagome metals near ideal Van Hove filling. Here, we use optical spectroscopy on $A$V$_3$Sb$_5$ with mixed $A$-site compositions to reveal the effect of the alkali metal on the low-energy electronic structure. Supported by density-functional-theory calculations, we identify a band-saddle-point inversion as a chemical consequence of Cs substitution, revealing that $A$-site composition controls the orbital character of Van Hove singularities, Fermi surface topology, and electron-phonon interactions while leaving the kagome layer intact.

AI.tldr: Optical spectroscopy on mixed A-site AV3Sb5 kagome metals reveals that A-site composition controls the orbital character of Van Hove singularities, Fermi surface topology, and electron-phonon interactions, driven by a band-saddle-point inversion upon Cs substitution.
AI.motivation: AV3Sb5 compounds (A = K, Rb, Cs) are a platform for kagome physics near ideal Van Hove filling, but the role of the alkali-metal A-site in tuning the low-energy electronic structure remains unclear.
AI.method: Optical spectroscopy on AV3Sb5 with mixed A-site compositions, supported by density-functional-theory (DFT) calculations.
AI.result: A band-saddle-point inversion is identified as a chemical consequence of Cs substitution.
AI.conclusion: A-site composition controls the orbital character of Van Hove singularities, Fermi surface topology, and electron-phonon interactions while leaving the kagome layer intact.

title: Towards a Metal-Organic Framework with Pore-Confined Electrons
summary: Electrides are an unconventional class of materials in which electrons are localized in crystallographic void spaces rather than solely around atomic nuclei, giving rise to appealing properties such as low work functions, strong electron-donating character, and even superconductivity. Here, we use ab initio methods to investigate metal-organic framework (MOF) electrides, a new class of materials that combines the interstitial electrons of electrides with the permanent porosity and chemical tunability of MOFs. These materials host pore-confined electrons: occupied electronic states localized in the pore space and with bands slightly below or crossing through the Fermi level. Using density functional theory calculations, we establish several design rules for stabilizing pore-confined electrons in MOFs via an anion-electron exchange process and identify candidate MOF electrides. As a proof-of-concept, we also demonstrate that the pore-confined electrons can directly facilitate chemical reactions, substantially lowering the activation barrier for H2 dissociation without requiring adsorption at a surface site. We envision that pore-confined electrons in nanoporous materials may enable a fundamentally new type of catalysis in which chemical reactions take place in the pore space, driven by electron-centered active sites.

AI.tldr: Ab initio DFT study of metal-organic framework (MOF) electrides hosting pore-confined electrons, establishing design rules and demonstrating catalytic H2 dissociation in the pore space.
AI.motivation: Electrides localize electrons in crystallographic voids, yielding low work functions, strong electron donation, and superconductivity; combining these interstitial electrons with the porosity and tunability of MOFs could yield a new class of materials with novel electron-centered reactivity.
AI.method: Ab initio / density functional theory calculations on MOF electrides; analysis of occupied electronic states in the pore space with bands near or crossing the Fermi level; formulation of design rules for stabilizing pore-confined electrons via an anion-electron exchange process; identification of candidate MOF electrides; proof-of-concept simulation of H2 dissociation mediated by pore-confined electrons.
AI.result: Pore-confined electrons are identified as occupied states localized in the pore volume with bands slightly below or crossing the Fermi level. Several design rules for stabilizing such electrons via anion-electron exchange are established, and candidate MOF electrides are identified. The pore-confined electrons substantially lower the activation barrier for H2 dissociation without requiring adsorption at a surface site.
AI.conclusion: Pore-confined electrons in nanoporous materials may enable a fundamentally new type of catalysis in which reactions occur directly in the pore space, driven by electron-centered active sites rather than conventional surface sites.

title: A self-compliant selector-free memory with functional bismuth ferrite
summary: In-memory computing requires selector-free operation, low variability, and stable multilevel switching, all of which remain challenging to achieve in a single system. Here, we demonstrate a robust selector-free memory based on a multiferroic BiFeO3 that combines self-compliance with stable bipolar switching, high yield, long endurance, and extended retention. We observe that BiFeO3 memristive crossbar arrays become self-compliant through a naturally formed TiOx interfacial layer, enabling forming-free bipolar switching without external selector devices, addressing major bottlenecks that have limited the practical deployment of resistive memories. The array delivers stable bipolar switching with a 97% device yield, endurance beyond 105 cycles, and data retention exceeding 105 s with low cycle-to-cycle and device-to-device variability. In addition, the devices exhibit 16 well-separated conductance states, enabling 4-bit multilevel operation via precise pulse-controlled programming for digit visualization in edge applications. Noise measurements reveal predominantly 1/f-type behavior with minimal random telegraph noise, indicating robust conductance stability across the programmable window. These results establish BiFeO3 as a practical materials platform for multibit, selector-free crossbar memories offering high reliability, making it well-suited for scalable computing architectures based on functional materials.

AI.tldr: A multiferroic BiFeO3 memristive crossbar array achieves selector-free, self-compliant bipolar switching via a naturally formed TiOx interfacial layer, delivering 97% yield, >10^5 endurance, >10^5 s retention, 4-bit multilevel operation, and low noise for scalable in-memory computing.
AI.motivation: In-memory computing requires selector-free operation, low variability, and stable multilevel switching, but achieving all these simultaneously in a single system remains challenging. Practical deployment of resistive memories is limited by the need for external selector devices and by variability/endurance issues.
AI.method: The authors fabricated a BiFeO3-based multiferroic memristive crossbar array. A naturally formed TiOx interfacial layer induces self-compliance, enabling forming-free bipolar switching without external selector devices. Device performance was characterized via yield, endurance, retention, multilevel pulse programming (16 conductance states for 4-bit operation), and noise measurements (1/f behavior and random telegraph noise).
AI.result: The array exhibits self-compliant, forming-free bipolar switching with 97% device yield, endurance beyond 10^5 cycles, and retention exceeding 10^5 s with low cycle-to-cycle and device-to-device variability. It provides 16 well-separated conductance states for 4-bit multilevel operation via pulse-controlled programming, enabling digit visualization in edge applications. Noise is predominantly 1/f-type with minimal random telegraph noise, indicating stable conductance across the programmable window.
AI.conclusion: BiFeO3 is established as a practical materials platform for multibit, selector-free crossbar memories with high reliability, well-suited for scalable computing architectures based on functional materials.

title: Twinning of domains and spin anisotropy in K$_5$Fe$_4$Ag$_6$Te$_{10}$
summary: The Fe-based superconductors are derived from metallic parent compounds with nematic and stripe magnetic orders, which lead to two types of magnetic domains. Recently it was found that K$_5$Fe$_4$Ag$_6$Te$_{10}$ (KFAT), an Fe-based semiconductor, exhibits similar nematic and stripe magnetic orders, and is thus an analogue to the Fe-based superconductors in the limit of localized electrons. In this work, the superstructure and magnetic domains of KFAT are elucidated by fully mapping the reciprocal space using time-of-flight single crystal neutron diffraction. In KFAT, Fe and Ag atoms order to form a $\sqrt{5}\times\sqrt{5}$ superstructure containing $2\times2$ Fe blocks, which leads to two superstructure domains with identical main Bragg peaks but distinct superstructure peaks. Below $T_{\rm N}\approx35$~K, magnetic and nematic orders break in-plane rotational symmetry of the tetragonal $\sqrt{5}\times\sqrt{5}$ superstructure, and further give rise to two magnetic domains. These four equally populated domains account for the complex scattering pattern observed in our time-of-flight elastic neutron scattering measurements. Using polarized neutron scattering, we demonstrate a prominent spin anisotropy with an easy-plane spanned by the $c$-axis and the intra-block antiferromagnetic Fe-Fe bond direction. Such an anisotropy at ${\bf q}\neq0$ persists well above $T_{\rm N}$, accounts for the in-plane ${\bf q}=0$ magnetic anisotropy observed in uniaxial-strained KFAT, and offers an indicator for discovering similar piezomagnetic effects in other materials.

AI.tldr: Time-of-flight and polarized neutron diffraction on K5Fe4Ag6Te10 (KFAT) reveal a √5×√5 superstructure with two superstructure domains, plus magnetic and nematic orders below T_N ≈ 35 K creating four equally populated domains and a pronounced easy-plane spin anisotropy that persists above T_N.
AI.motivation: KFAT is an Fe-based semiconductor analogue to Fe-based superconductors in the localized-electron limit, exhibiting nematic and stripe magnetic orders. Its superstructure and magnetic domain structure were previously unresolved, and understanding them is key to linking localized-electron physics to the nematicity and magnetic anisotropy of Fe-based superconductors.
AI.method: Time-of-flight single-crystal neutron diffraction for full reciprocal-space mapping; time-of-flight elastic neutron scattering to characterize the domain-related scattering pattern; polarized neutron scattering to probe spin anisotropy.
AI.result: Fe and Ag order into a √5×√5 superstructure containing 2×2 Fe blocks, producing two superstructure domains with identical main Bragg peaks but distinct superstructure peaks. Below T_N ≈ 35 K, magnetic and nematic orders break the in-plane rotational symmetry of the tetragonal √5×√5 superstructure, yielding two magnetic domains; the four equally populated domains explain the complex scattering pattern. A prominent spin anisotropy with an easy-plane defined by the c-axis and the intra-block antiferromagnetic Fe-Fe bond direction is observed at q ≠ 0 and persists well above T_N.
AI.conclusion: The four-domain picture (two superstructure + two magnetic domains) fully accounts for the observed scattering. The q ≠ 0 spin anisotropy persists above T_N, explains the in-plane q = 0 magnetic anisotropy in uniaxial-strained KFAT, and provides an indicator for discovering similar piezomagnetic effects in other materials.

title: Effects of residual exchange coupling on simultaneously driven spin qubits
summary: Exchange coupling and microwave drives are widely used control mechanisms for spin qubits. However, the influence of exchange coupling on microwave-driven spin dynamics is not fully understood. We report simultaneous drive measurements of two spin qubits as a function of exchange coupling and drive power. When the Rabi frequency exceeds exchange, we observe a beating pattern in the Rabi oscillations. In the opposite limit, two exchange-split patterns emerge in the Rabi chevrons. We find that these exchange-induced effects are suppressed when the difference in the Rabi frequencies exceeds the exchange coupling. A theoretical model is developed that reproduces the main features in our data.

AI.tldr: Simultaneous microwave drive of two exchange-coupled spin qubits reveals exchange-induced beating and split Rabi chevrons, suppressed when the Rabi-frequency difference exceeds the exchange coupling.
AI.motivation: Exchange coupling and microwave drives are both widely used spin-qubit control mechanisms, yet the influence of exchange coupling on microwave-driven spin dynamics remains incompletely understood.
AI.method: Simultaneous drive measurements of two spin qubits as a function of exchange coupling and drive power, supported by a theoretical model reproducing the main experimental features.
AI.result: When the Rabi frequency exceeds the exchange coupling, a beating pattern appears in the Rabi oscillations. In the opposite limit, two exchange-split patterns emerge in the Rabi chevrons. These exchange-induced effects are suppressed when the difference in Rabi frequencies exceeds the exchange coupling.
AI.conclusion: Exchange coupling qualitatively reshapes microwave-driven spin dynamics, producing distinct beating and exchange-split signatures in the two limiting regimes, with a theoretical model capturing the observed behavior.

title: Engineering Competing Fractional Topological States in a BHZ Superlattice
summary: Scalar superlattices offer a route from simple topological bands to fractionalized states, while multicomponent systems raise the additional question of which fractional order is energetically selected. We show that a scalar superlattice applied to the Qi-Wu-Zhang (QWZ) Chern-insulator model produces an isolated C = +1 miniband with strongly improved Berry-curvature and quantum metric uniformity. Exact diagonalization of the projected interaction identifies a 1/3 fractional Chern insulator in this miniband. Restoring the time-reversed partner to form the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang (BHZ) superlattice yields, at total filling 2/3, a balanced fractional quantum spin Hall (FQSH)-like state and a fully polarized 2/3 fractional Chern insulator. Their competition separates two aspects of fractional-state control: the finite-momentum intercomponent coupling governs the stability of the balanced FQSH-like state, whereas a uniform pseudospin anisotropy shifts the relative energies of conserved sectors and can switch the global ground state between the balanced and polarized states. These results establish a minimal lattice setting that connects topological-miniband reconstruction, fractional-state formation, and fractional-state selection, illustrating how distinct levels of control can be combined to navigate competing fractional topological states.

AI.tldr: A scalar superlattice applied to the QWZ Chern insulator produces a uniform isolated C=+1 miniband hosting a 1/3 fractional Chern insulator; extending to the BHZ superlattice reveals a competition between a balanced FQSH-like state and a fully polarized 2/3 FCI at total filling 2/3.
AI.motivation: Multicomponent topological systems raise the question of which fractional order is energetically selected, and a minimal lattice setting connecting topological-miniband reconstruction, fractional-state formation, and fractional-state selection is needed.
AI.method: A scalar superlattice is applied to the Qi-Wu-Zhang (QWZ) Chern-insulator model to engineer an isolated C = +1 miniband with improved Berry-curvature and quantum metric uniformity; exact diagonalization of the projected interaction is used to identify fractional states. The time-reversed partner is then restored to form the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang (BHZ) superlattice, and the competition between candidate states is analyzed.
AI.result: A 1/3 fractional Chern insulator is found in the QWZ miniband. In the BHZ superlattice at total filling 2/3, a balanced fractional quantum spin Hall (FQSH)-like state and a fully polarized 2/3 fractional Chern insulator compete: finite-momentum intercomponent coupling governs the stability of the balanced FQSH-like state, while uniform pseudospin anisotropy shifts the relative energies of conserved sectors and can switch the global ground state.
AI.conclusion: The results establish a minimal lattice setting connecting topological-miniband reconstruction, fractional-state formation, and fractional-state selection, showing how distinct levels of control can be combined to navigate competing fractional topological states.

title: Exchange-Driven Chiral Magnons and Weyl States in Room-Temperature Metallic XCoB$_2$ (X= Ta, Zr and Hf) Altermagnets
summary: Metallic altermagnets remain rare, particularly in low-symmetry three-dimensional crystals where spin-split electronic bands and chiral magnon excitations can coexist. We report a family of metallic $d_{yz}$-wave altermagnets in the orthorhombic ternary borides XCoB$_2$ (X = Ta, Zr, Hf), which crystallize in the centrosymmetric $Pnma$ structure with G-type collinear magnetic order. Symmetry analysis within the magnetic space group $Pnm'a'$ (BNS No.~62.447) predicts a nonrelativistic spin splitting proportional to $k_yk_z$, with symmetry-enforced degeneracy on the $k_y$ and $k_z$ nodal planes, consistent with first-principles calculations. On the $k_x=0$ plane, the momentum-averaged spin splitting reaches 88.4, 52.3, and 70.6~meV at the Fermi level in TaCoB$_2$, ZrCoB$_2$, and HfCoB$_2$, respectively, with maxima exceeding 200~meV in all three compounds. Exchange analysis shows that the altermagnetic magnon splitting originates from symmetry-inequivalent sixth-neighbour inter-sublattice interactions. The chirality splitting reaches 1.51, 2.03, and 3.10 meV below 50 meV in TaCoB$_2$, ZrCoB$_2$, and HfCoB$_2$, respectively, making it accessible to inelastic neutron scattering. Monte Carlo simulations yield N'eel temperatures of $67\pm1.1$, $330\pm5.7$, and $307\pm5.0$~K, placing ZrCoB$_2$ and HfCoB$*2$ above room temperature. With spin-orbit coupling included, all three compounds host symmetry-protected Weyl points near the Fermi level, Fermi-arc surface states and sizable intrinsic anomalous Hall conductivities $σ*{zx}$ of $+342$, $-392$, and $-221$~S/cm at the Fermi level, reaching maximum magnitudes of $763$, $942$, and $924$~S/cm for TaCoB$_2$, ZrCoB$_2$, and HfCoB$_2$, respectively. $X$CoB$_2$ therefore provides a single compensated platform carrying both magnonic and electronic chirality, one in the spin waves and the other in the Berry curvature, without any stray field.

AI.tldr: The paper reports a family of metallic d_yz-wave altermagnets XCoB2 (X = Ta, Zr, Hf) in the centrosymmetric Pnma structure, hosting spin-split bands, chiral magnons, Weyl points, and large anomalous Hall conductivities.
AI.motivation: Metallic altermagnets are rare, especially in low-symmetry 3D crystals where spin-split electronic bands and chiral magnon excitations can coexist, motivating the search for a single platform combining these properties without stray fields.
AI.method: Symmetry analysis within magnetic space group Pnm'a' (BNS No. 62.447), first-principles calculations, exchange analysis, Monte Carlo simulations, and spin-orbit coupling calculations to examine band splitting, magnon chirality, and topological/Berry-curvature features.
AI.result: Nonrelativistic spin splitting proportional to k_y k_z with nodal-plane degeneracy; momentum-averaged splitting at Fermi level of 88.4/52.3/70.6 meV (maxima >200 meV). Chirality splitting up to 1.51/2.03/3.10 meV. Neel temperatures 67±1.1/330±5.7/307±5.0 K. Weyl points, Fermi-arc surface states, and intrinsic anomalous Hall conductivities σ_zx of +342/-392/-221 S/cm (max 763/942/924 S/cm).
AI.conclusion: XCoB2 provides a single compensated platform carrying both magnonic chirality (in spin waves) and electronic chirality (in Berry curvature) without stray field, with ZrCoB2 and HfCoB2 above room temperature.

title: Induced superconductivity in selective-area grown SnTe devices
summary: Topological superconductors are of high interest for applications in topological quantum computation. The required topologically superconducting state can be engineered by proximityinducing superconductivity in a topological insulator. Here, we explore the induced superconductivity in selective-area grown nanowires of the topological crystalline insulator SnTe on a InP substrate, through TEM/EDX and low-temperature electronic transport studies. The observed superconducting behavior likely originates from indium in the substrate diffusing upwards into the SnTe nanowire, forming a thin layer of InxSn1-xTe at the interface between the nanowire and the substrate. InxSn1-xTe is intrinsically superconducting for indium concentrations above 2%, resulting in superconductivity within the heterostructure. Little-Parks oscillations are observed in loop-shaped nanowire networks in an out-of-plane magnetic field. The half-period shift indicative of a topological superconducting state is absent, which is explained by dominant trivial transport channels obscuring any topological signatures.

AI.tldr: Indium diffusion from an InP substrate into SnTe nanowires creates a superconducting InxSn1-xTe interfacial layer, producing superconductivity in the heterostructure.
AI.motivation: Topological superconductors are highly desirable for topological quantum computation, and proximity-inducing superconductivity in a topological insulator is a promising route toward the required topological superconducting state.
AI.method: The authors studied selective-area-grown nanowires of the topological crystalline insulator SnTe on InP using TEM/EDX and low-temperature electronic transport measurements, including Little-Parks experiments on loop-shaped nanowire networks in an out-of-plane magnetic field.
AI.result: The observed superconductivity likely arises from indium diffusing upward from the substrate into the SnTe nanowire, forming an interfacial InxSn1-xTe layer, which is intrinsically superconducting for In concentrations above 2%. Little-Parks oscillations are observed, but the half-period shift characteristic of a topological superconducting state is absent.
AI.conclusion: The absence of the half-period shift is attributed to dominant trivial transport channels that obscure any topological signatures. The heterostructure is therefore not established as a topological superconductor.

title: Fractional vortices in a spin-isotropic spiral spin liquid
summary: Spiral spin liquids are magnetic states whose classical ground-state manifold consists of planar incommensurate spin spirals with wave vectors lying on a continuous ring or surface in reciprocal space. The resulting subextensive degeneracy suppresses magnetic long-range order and gives rise to liquid-like behavior. Despite numerous material realizations and theoretical investigations, the structure of low-temperature spin configurations of spin-isotropic Heisenberg spiral spin liquids has remained poorly understood. Here, we classify and characterize the classical topological defects supported by these systems. We uncover a rich family of vortex types involving concerted windings of spin directions, spiral-plane normals, and wave-vector orientations, yielding a $\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_2$ classification. Remarkably, the elementary defects are half-vortices carrying fractional $2π$ windings in both spin and momentum space and obey fusion rules resembling to those of Ising anyons. Large-scale classical simulations of a square-lattice spiral spin liquid reveal that these vortices are dense in the spiral-spin-liquid regime, and bind tightly below an order-by-disorder phase transition, eventually fusing to vacuum.

AI.tldr: This work classifies the classical topological defects of spin-isotropic Heisenberg spiral spin liquids, revealing a rich family of vortices with a Z x Z2 classification, whose elementary half-vortices carry fractional 2π windings in spin and momentum space and obey Ising-anyon-like fusion rules, and shows via large-scale simulations that these vortices are dense in the spiral-spin-liquid regime and bind tightly below an order-by-disorder transition.
AI.motivation: Spiral spin liquids exhibit a subextensive ground-state degeneracy from planar incommensurate spin spirals whose wave vectors lie on a continuous ring or surface in reciprocal space, suppressing long-range order. Despite many material realizations and theoretical studies, the structure of low-temperature spin configurations in spin-isotropic Heisenberg spiral spin liquids remained poorly understood.
AI.method: The authors classify and characterize the classical topological defects supported by spin-isotropic Heisenberg spiral spin liquids, analyzing the concerted windings of spin directions, spiral-plane normals, and wave-vector orientations. They also perform large-scale classical simulations of a square-lattice spiral spin liquid.
AI.result: They uncover a rich family of vortex types yielding a Z x Z2 classification. The elementary defects are half-vortices carrying fractional 2π windings in both spin and momentum space and obey fusion rules resembling those of Ising anyons. Simulations show these vortices are dense in the spiral-spin-liquid regime and bind tightly below an order-by-disorder phase transition, eventually fusing to vacuum.
AI.conclusion: The elementary fractional half-vortices with Ising-anyon-like fusion rules provide a topological characterization of spin-isotropic Heisenberg spiral spin liquids, with the dense vortex picture and their binding at the order-by-disorder transition offering a framework for understanding the low-temperature behavior and possible fractionalized excitations of these frustrated magnets.

title: Ultrafast Magnetization Induced from Raman-Active Axial Chiral Phonons
summary: Axial chiral phonons, which carry angular momentum and exhibit unusually large magnetic moments, provide a new degree of freedom for controlling the time-reversal symmetry and magnetic properties of quantum materials. While infrared-active axial phonons are efficiently excited to large amplitudes by circularly polarized terahertz pulses, their application may be constrained by short lifetimes, small penetration depths, low spatial resolution, and limited availability of optical sources. Here, we report that an axial Raman-active phonon mode in CeF3 exhibits a significant magnetic moment and an exceedingly long lifetime that more closely matches the paramagnetic spin dynamics. The axial phonon population is resonantly driven by a near-infrared laser pulse with rotating linear polarization, known as an optical centrifuge, a coherent control scheme never applied to solids before. The phonon-driven magnetization observed by time-resolved Faraday rotation scales quadratically with incident power and rapidly decreases at high temperatures, consistent with phonon inverse Faraday effect from many-body spin-phonon coupling. Our findings open a new avenue for using shaped laser pulses from widely accessible light sources to manipulate coherent axial chiral phonons and ultrafast spintronics.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that an axial Raman-active phonon in CeF3, driven by an optical centrifuge, exhibits a large magnetic moment and long lifetime, enabling phonon-driven magnetization via the inverse Faraday effect.
AI.motivation: Axial chiral phonons offer a new degree of freedom for controlling time-reversal symmetry and magnetic properties, but infrared-active axial phonons are limited by short lifetimes, small penetration depths, low spatial resolution, and scarce optical sources. The authors seek a more practical alternative.
AI.method: The axial Raman-active phonon mode in CeF3 is resonantly driven by a near-infrared laser pulse with rotating linear polarization (an optical centrifuge), a coherent control scheme applied to solids for the first time. Phonon-driven magnetization is probed by time-resolved Faraday rotation.
AI.result: The driven axial phonon exhibits a significant magnetic moment and an exceptionally long lifetime matching paramagnetic spin dynamics. The magnetization scales quadratically with incident power and decreases rapidly at high temperatures, consistent with the phonon inverse Faraday effect arising from many-body spin-phonon coupling.
AI.conclusion: Shaped laser pulses from widely accessible light sources can manipulate coherent axial chiral phonons, opening a new avenue for ultrafast spintronics.

title: Shot noise signatures of Majorana-assisted transport in an Aharonov-Bohm interferometer
summary: In this work, we investigate the finite-bias charge current, shot noise, and Fano factor in an Aharonov-Bohm interferometer composed of two parallel quantum dots, each side-coupled to a topological superconducting nanowire represented by an effective Kitaev chain hosting Majorana bound states at its ends. The transport properties are calculated using the nonequilibrium Green's function formalism within the equation-of-motion approach. Our results show that coupling to the Majorana bound states significantly modifies the interference pattern, producing distinctive signatures in the current, shot noise, and Fano factor. These signatures are particularly pronounced at the half-flux condition, where destructive interference suppresses the conventional transport background and enhances the visibility of Majorana-assisted transport. These findings demonstrate that finite-bias shot-noise spectroscopy provides a sensitive indirect probe of Majorana bound states in hybrid superconducting-nanowire interferometers.

AI.tldr: Finite-bias shot-noise spectroscopy of an Aharonov-Bohm interferometer with two quantum dots side-coupled to Majorana nanowires reveals distinctive signatures of Majorana bound states, most pronounced at half-flux.
AI.motivation: To establish a sensitive indirect probe of Majorana bound states (MBSs) in hybrid superconducting-nanowire interferometers, since conventional transport signatures are often obscured by trivial background contributions.
AI.method: Finite-bias charge current, shot noise, and Fano factor are computed for an Aharonov-Bohm interferometer of two parallel quantum dots, each side-coupled to a topological superconducting nanowire modeled as an effective Kitaev chain with end Majorana modes. Calculations use the nonequilibrium Green's function formalism within the equation-of-motion approach.
AI.result: Coupling to Majorana bound states significantly modifies the interference pattern, yielding distinctive signatures in the current, shot noise, and Fano factor. The signatures are particularly pronounced at the half-flux condition, where destructive interference suppresses the conventional transport background and enhances the visibility of Majorana-assisted transport.
AI.conclusion: Finite-bias shot-noise spectroscopy provides a sensitive indirect probe of Majorana bound states in hybrid superconducting-nanowire interferometers.

title: Effect of Near-surface Thermal Spikes on Radiation Hardness of Gallium Oxide
summary: Gallium oxide (Ga$_{2}$O$_{3}$) stands out as an extraordinary high radiation-tolerant semiconductor, because its lattice displacements induce polymorph transitions, holding material crystalline instead of leading to amorphization. Meanwhile, under extremely severe irradiation conditions many crystals become amorphous, often starting from surfaces where the translation symmetry breaks. Here, we show that the surface amorphization may prevail over the crystallisation in Ga$_{2}$O$_{3}$, however only if the mass and energy of irradiated ions produce sufficiently dense heat spikes in the immediate vicinity of the free surface. Applying machine-learned molecular dynamics simulations together with experimental broad-beam and focused ion-beam irradiations, we conclude that the presence of the free surface enables asymmetric displacements of Ga and O atoms, leading to a local non-stoichiometry. Consequently, when the affected cascade volume is sufficiently large, this compositional imbalance suppresses recrystallization and promotes amorphization. As such, our results are ready to use for tailoring irradiation conditions to either prevent or induce surface amorphization, depending on the requirements of the intended applications in Ga$_{2}$O$_{3}$ or other compound semiconductors.

AI.tldr: Ga2O3 normally resists amorphization via irradiation-induced polymorph transitions, but free surfaces can reverse this: sufficiently dense ion heat spikes near the surface cause asymmetric Ga/O displacements and local non-stoichiometry that suppress recrystallization and promote surface amorphization.
AI.motivation: Ga2O3 is prized as a highly radiation-tolerant semiconductor because lattice displacements trigger polymorph transitions rather than amorphization, yet under severe irradiation many crystals do become amorphous—often nucleating at surfaces where translational symmetry is broken. The paper aims to resolve when and why surface amorphization can dominate over recrystallization in Ga2O3.
AI.method: Machine-learned molecular dynamics simulations combined with experimental broad-beam and focused ion-beam irradiations were used to probe ion-mass- and energy-dependent damage near free surfaces.
AI.result: Surface amorphization prevails over crystallization only when the irradiated ions' mass and energy generate sufficiently dense heat spikes in the immediate vicinity of the free surface. The free surface enables asymmetric displacements of Ga and O atoms, producing local non-stoichiometry; when the affected cascade volume is large enough, this compositional imbalance suppresses recrystallization and promotes amorphization.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide a predictive basis for tailoring irradiation conditions to either prevent or induce surface amorphization, as required by intended applications in Ga2O3 and potentially other compound semiconductors.

title: Cryothermal Measurements of Variable-Emittance Coatings with Lower Phase Transition Temperatures for Space Thermal Control
summary: Space thermal control is critically important to ensure proper operation of on-board equipment in a regulated temperature range. Passive thermal control with variable-emittance coatings (VECs) could help save power consumption in a dynamically changing space thermal environment. Vanadium dioxide (VO2) based VECs have been studied for space thermal control but its intrinsic phase transition around 68°C limits its wider space applications where lower temperature ranges are expected. In this work, we experimentally demonstrate enhanced radiative heat dissipation in space-like thermal environment via cryothermal measurements with VECs of undoped and tungsten doped VO2. The fabricated undoped VEC exhibits a large emittance change of 0.6 across the phase transition, while the 1 at.% tungsten doped one shows an appreciable emittance variable of 0.4 with phase transition temperature lowered by 25°C. A vacuum cryothermal setup is developed with a liquid nitrogen cooled coldfinger to mimic cold space thermal background and a custom-designed sample mount suspended by nylon wires. After careful calibration and validation, greatly enhanced radiative heat dissipation upon VO2 phase transition up to 3.5 times with transition temperature lowered by 25°C from 1 at.% tungsten doping is clearly observed from the cryothermal tests. In the actual space thermal environment, radiative heat flux could further increase across phase transition from 160 W/m2 to 650 W/m2 with undoped VO2 coating from 55°C to 80°C, and from 175 W/m2 to 493 W/m2 with 1 at.% tungsten doped VEC from 30°C to 55°C.

AI.tldr: Undoped and W-doped VO2 variable-emittance coatings were tested in a vacuum cryothermal setup mimicking cold space, showing large emittance changes and up to 3.5x enhanced radiative heat dissipation with the transition temperature lowered by 25°C via 1 at.% W doping.
AI.motivation: Space thermal control is critical for on-board equipment, and passive variable-emittance coatings (VECs) can save power in dynamic space thermal environments. VO2-based VECs are promising but their intrinsic phase transition near 68°C is too high for many space applications requiring lower temperature ranges.
AI.method: Fabricated undoped and 1 at.% tungsten-doped VO2 VECs, and developed a vacuum cryothermal setup with a liquid-nitrogen-cooled coldfinger to mimic cold space background plus a custom sample mount suspended by nylon wires. Performed careful calibration/validation and cryothermal measurements of radiative heat dissipation across the phase transition.
AI.result: Undoped VEC showed a large emittance change of 0.6 across the transition; 1 at.% W-doped VEC showed an emittance variable of 0.4 with transition temperature lowered by 25°C. Cryothermal tests revealed up to 3.5x enhanced radiative heat dissipation upon VO2 phase transition with the doping-lowered transition temperature. In actual space thermal environment, radiative heat flux could increase from 160 to 650 W/m2 (undoped VO2, 55–80°C) and from 175 to 493 W/m2 (1 at.% W-doped, 30–55°C).
AI.conclusion: Tungsten doping effectively lowers the VO2 phase transition temperature while retaining appreciable emittance variability, enabling greatly enhanced radiative heat dissipation in space-like thermal environments and making VO2-based VECs viable for lower-temperature space thermal control applications.

title: How Accurately Can We Describe Spin Crossover?
summary: The complicated physicochemical properties of metal complexes that exhibit thermal spin crossover make it difficult for routine electronic structure calculations to yield an accurate transition temperature prediction, $T_{1/2}$. The difficulty lies in the intricate connection between the spin-crossover energy, which is a molecular spectroscopic property, and $T_{1/2}$, a condensed phase property. Here we show how to obtain spin-crossover energies systematically by reverse engineering of experimental $T_{1/2}$ data. The protocol is based upon fitting the range separation parameter, $ω$, in the hybrid LC-$ω$PBE density functional to reproduce the experimental $T_{1/2}$ values for a series of metal complexes. We provide insights into the sources of variations of at least $\pm 15$ kJ mol$^{-1}$ found from common exchange and correlation functionals by comparing their performance against our reference data. By analysis of the sensitivity of transition temperatures to $\pm 1$ \% shifts in the range separation parameter, we determined a typical uncertainty of $\pm 50$ K for them, and a $\pm 2$ kJ mol$^{-1}$ uncertainty in the extracted spin-crossover energies due to $\pm 1$ \% variations of $T_{1/2}$. Lastly, we present results from the high-level, all-electron coupled cluster method for eight of the smaller molecules in the reference data set, and discuss the influence of the truncation of the excitation series upon the spin state energies.

AI.tldr: Reverse-engineering experimental T1/2 data via tuning the range-separation parameter ω in LC-ωPBE yields systematic spin-crossover energies, quantifies functional uncertainty at ±15 kJ/mol, and establishes ~±50 K T1/2 and ±2 kJ/mol coupling-constant uncertainties.
AI.motivation: Thermal spin crossover (SCO) in metal complexes couples a molecular spectroscopic property (spin-crossover energy) to a condensed-phase observable (T1/2), so routine electronic structure calculations struggle to predict transition temperatures accurately. Existing exchange-correlation functionals disagree by at least ±15 kJ/mol, and there is no systematic route to calibrate spin-crossover energies against experiment.
AI.method: The authors obtain spin-crossover energies by reverse engineering experimental T1/2 data. They fit the range-separation parameter ω in the hybrid LC-ωPBE density functional to reproduce measured T1/2 values across a series of metal complexes, then benchmark common exchange and correlation functionals against these reference data. Sensitivity analysis quantifies how ±1% shifts in ω propagate to T1/2 and to the extracted spin-crossover energies. High-level all-electron coupled cluster calculations are performed for eight smaller molecules in the data set to assess the effect of truncating the excitation series on spin-state energies.
AI.result: Fitting ω in LC-ωPBE reproduces experimental T1/2 values and provides reference spin-crossover energies. Common exchange and correlation functionals deviate by at least ±15 kJ/mol from these references. A ±1% variation in the range-separation parameter corresponds to a typical T1/2 uncertainty of ±50 K and a spin-crossover energy uncertainty of ±2 kJ/mol. Coupled cluster results for eight smaller complexes reveal how truncation of the excitation series affects spin-state energy splittings.
AI.conclusion: Tuning the range-separation parameter ω offers a systematic, experimentally anchored protocol for extracting spin-crossover energies and diagnosing functional-dependent errors. The derived uncertainty relations (±50 K per ±1% ω; ±2 kJ/mol per ±1% T1/2) provide practical error bars, while coupled cluster benchmarks indicate that excitation-series truncation must be controlled when computing spin-state energetics.

title: Time- and Frequency-Resolved Observation of Inverse Orbital Hall Effect in Gallium Nitride via Terahertz Polarimetry
summary: Orbitronics has attracted significant attention as a platform for information storage and processing that exploits the orbital angular momentum (OAM) of electrons without the need for spin-orbit coupling. However, experimental evaluation of OAM-charge interconversion remains a challenge and the results are often controversial due to the coexistence of bulk and interfacial contributions and the complexity in sample structures. Here, using circularly polarized light pulses and terahertz (THz) polarimetry, we developed a non-contact method to observe the inverse orbital Hall effect as a bulk response within a single material without employing heterostructure samples. In a semiconductor GaN, we directly captured the OAM-to-charge current conversion of holes in the THz frequency range. By analyzing the sharp frequency dependence of the Hall conductivity, we disentangled the competing microscopic mechanisms and revealed the dominant role of extrinsic contributions to the orbital Hall effect in the dc limit. By contrast, the Hall conductivity at THz frequencies above the impurity scattering rate is attributed to the intrinsic Berry-curvature mechanism,allowing a quantitative comparison with the microscopic theory. Furthermore, the ultrafast dynamics of the inverse orbital Hall signal directly revealed sub-picosecond OAM relaxation of holes, comparable to that of phonon-mediated thermalization. The quantitative argument based on theoretical calculations suggested the existence of an even faster decay channel due to momentum redistribution by acoustic phonons, suggesting a sub-nanometer-scale OAM relaxation length. Our results provide comprehensive and crucial insights into OAM transport and establish an ultrafast, contact-free approach for investigating OAM-to-charge conversion.

AI.tldr: Using circularly polarized THz pulses and polarimetry on bulk GaN, the authors observe the inverse orbital Hall effect non-contactly, disentangle intrinsic and extrinsic contributions, and reveal sub-picosecond orbital angular momentum relaxation of holes.
AI.motivation: Orbitronics is promising for information storage and processing using electron orbital angular momentum (OAM) without spin-orbit coupling, but experimental evaluation of OAM-charge interconversion is difficult and controversial because bulk and interfacial contributions coexist and sample structures are complex. A method is needed to isolate the bulk OAM response in a single material.
AI.method: Circularly polarized light pulses combined with terahertz (THz) polarimetry were used as a non-contact, heterostructure-free probe to measure the inverse orbital Hall effect as a bulk response in a single semiconductor, GaN. The OAM-to-charge current conversion of holes was captured in the THz frequency range, and the sharp frequency dependence of the Hall conductivity was analyzed to separate competing microscopic mechanisms.
AI.result: The inverse orbital Hall effect was directly observed in bulk GaN via THz OAM-to-charge conversion of holes. Frequency-dependent Hall conductivity analysis showed that extrinsic contributions dominate the orbital Hall effect in the dc limit, whereas above the impurity scattering rate the response is governed by the intrinsic Berry-curvature mechanism, enabling quantitative comparison with microscopic theory. Ultrafast dynamics revealed sub-picosecond OAM relaxation of holes, comparable to phonon-mediated thermalization, with theoretical arguments suggesting an even faster decay channel from acoustic-phonon momentum redistribution and a sub-nanometer OAM relaxation length.
AI.conclusion: The work provides comprehensive insight into OAM transport and establishes an ultrafast, contact-free approach for investigating OAM-to-charge conversion, while clarifying the intrinsic versus extrinsic nature of the orbital Hall effect and the ultrafast relaxation of OAM in a bulk semiconductor.

title: Interfacial Engineering Enabled High-Resolution Stretchable Metal-Level Conductive Lines and Transparent Conductor
summary: As stretchable electronics advance toward higher integration density and finer feature sizes, stretchable conductors, which serve as the architectural backbone of these electronics, must be scaled down accordingly. However, achieving both high stretchability and high electrical conductivity at high resolution remains a challenge using existing conductive materials. Here, through material design and interfacial engineering, we develop a thiol-functionalized conducting polymer/gold hybrid stack that can be patterned down to 4 micrometer linewidths using standard photolithography, while maintaining high stretchability, metal-like conductivity (>40,000 S/cm), and environmental stability. Leveraging this capability, we demonstrate grid-based stretchable transparent electrodes that surpass the figure-of-merit of indium tin oxide, as well as a 1000-pixel-per-inch image interconnected with stretchable lines. This work helps to broaden the scope of next-generation functional soft electronics, including e-skins and bioelectronics.

AI.tldr: A thiol-functionalized conducting polymer/gold hybrid stack enables 4 µm-patternable stretchable conductors with metal-like conductivity (>40,000 S/cm) and environmental stability.
AI.motivation: Stretchable electronics are advancing toward higher integration density and finer feature sizes, so stretchable conductors must scale down accordingly. However, existing conductive materials struggle to simultaneously achieve high stretchability, high electrical conductivity, and high resolution.
AI.method: Through material design and interfacial engineering, the authors developed a thiol-functionalized conducting polymer/gold hybrid stack that can be patterned down to 4 µm linewidths using standard photolithography.
AI.result: The hybrid stack maintains high stretchability, metal-like conductivity (>40,000 S/cm), and environmental stability. It enabled grid-based stretchable transparent electrodes surpassing the figure-of-merit of indium tin oxide, and a 1000-pixel-per-inch image interconnected with stretchable lines.
AI.conclusion: This work broadens the scope of next-generation functional soft electronics, including e-skins and bioelectronics.

title: Probing the anomalous symmetry-breaking in kagome material CsV3Sb5 via third-order nonlinearity
summary: The kagome material has rapidly established itself as a research frontier in condensed matter physics, owing to its distinctive geometric structure and the rich array of unconventional physical phenomena. In the kagome AV3Sb5 (A = K, Rb, Cs) family, the charge-ordered state exhibits a remarkable characteristic, i.e., anomalous symmetry-breaking, which is tied to the topological nature of the electronic band structure. Here, we report the third-order nonlinear longitudinal and Hall responses that persist stably up to room temperature in the kagome material CsV3Sb5. Notably, the nonlinear responses demonstrate significant enhancement below the charge density wave (~ 77 K) order and anomalous symmetry-breaking (~ 39 K) state. The scaling analysis indicates that the third-order nonlinear transport is governed jointly by quantum geometric contribution and extrinsic scattering. This study realizes a giant third-order nonlinear response and provides a distinct method to detect anomalous symmetry-breaking in CsV3Sb5.

AI.tldr: This paper reports giant third-order nonlinear longitudinal and Hall responses in the kagome material CsV3Sb5 that persist up to room temperature and are strongly enhanced below the charge density wave (~77 K) and anomalous symmetry-breaking (~39 K) states.
AI.motivation: Kagome materials, particularly the AV3Sb5 family, host unconventional physics such as anomalous symmetry-breaking tied to topological band structure. However, sensitive probes of this anomalous symmetry-breaking are needed; the authors are motivated to explore nonlinear transport as a novel detection method.
AI.method: The authors measure third-order nonlinear longitudinal and Hall responses in CsV3Sb5 as a function of temperature, and perform scaling analysis to disentangle the underlying mechanisms.
AI.result: The third-order nonlinear responses are stable up to room temperature and show significant enhancement below the charge density wave (~77 K) order and the anomalous symmetry-breaking (~39 K) state. Scaling analysis indicates the third-order nonlinear transport is governed jointly by quantum geometric contributions and extrinsic scattering.
AI.conclusion: The work realizes a giant third-order nonlinear response in CsV3Sb5 and establishes nonlinear transport as a distinct method to detect anomalous symmetry-breaking in kagome materials.

title: Multi4D: an end-to-end neural network for structural determination at complex material interfaces
summary: Heterogeneous interfaces dictate the performance and degradation of functional materials, making it essential to link local structural variations with macroscopic failure mechanisms to guide future materials design. Yet structural heterogeneity, phase overlap, and local disorder produce highly convoluted diffraction signatures, making extended transition regions difficult to interpret at atomic resolution across large fields of view. Here, we introduce Multi4D, a physics-informed neural network framework for automated multi-component crystallographic identification using four-dimensional scanning transmission electron microscopy (4D-STEM). By combining a latent-space Diffusion Transformer for physics-constrained style translation with a rotation-invariant convolutional neural network for orientation-agnostic classification, this approach translates multi-components diffraction datasets into deterministic crystallographic maps with 98.82% accuracy. In addition, we introduce Diffraction-Inferred Structural Complexity as an information-theoretic entropy metric derived from classifier predictive uncertainty that quantifies local structural ambiguity. We apply Multi4D to generate high-fidelity structural maps of complex superconducting heterostructures, corroded alloy surfaces, and degraded solid-state battery interfaces down to single-nanometer spatial resolution. This framework establishes a statistically robust analytical paradigm for automated microscopy, facilitating both industrial quality control and the data-driven discovery of interfacial design principles.

AI.tldr: Multi4D is a physics-informed neural network framework for automated multi-component crystallographic identification using 4D-STEM, combining a latent-space Diffusion Transformer for physics-constrained style translation and a rotation-invariant CNN for orientation-agnostic classification, achieving 98.82% accuracy and introducing "Diffraction-Inferred Structural Complexity" as an entropy metric from classifier uncertainty, applied to superconducting heterostructures, corroded alloys, and degraded battery interfaces at single-nanometer resolution.
AI.motivation: Heterogeneous interfaces govern the performance and degradation of functional materials, so linking local structural variations to macroscopic failure mechanisms is essential for materials design. However, structural heterogeneity, phase overlap, and local disorder generate highly convoluted diffraction signatures, making extended transition regions difficult to interpret at atomic resolution across large fields of view.
AI.method: Multi4D is a physics-informed neural network framework for automated multi-component crystallographic identification from 4D-STEM data. It couples a latent-space Diffusion Transformer performing physics-constrained style translation with a rotation-invariant convolutional neural network for orientation-agnostic classification, translating multi-component diffraction datasets into deterministic crystallographic maps. Additionally, Diffraction-Inferred Structural Complexity is introduced as an information-theoretic entropy metric derived from classifier predictive uncertainty to quantify local structural ambiguity.
AI.result: The framework produces deterministic crystallographic maps with 98.82% accuracy and yields high-fidelity structural maps of complex superconducting heterostructures, corroded alloy surfaces, and degraded solid-state battery interfaces down to single-nanometer spatial resolution.
AI.conclusion: Multi4D establishes a statistically robust analytical paradigm for automated microscopy, supporting industrial quality control and data-driven discovery of interfacial design principles.

title: Bilinear magnon--exciton coupling in biased ferromagnetic electron--hole bilayers
summary: Two-dimensional magnetic semiconductors provide a unique platform where strong magnon--exciton interactions can be realized. Owing to the intrinsic energy mismatch between excitons and magnons, however, these interactions are typically between the exciton density and magnons. We propose biased ferromagnetic electron--hole bilayers, where the exciton energy gap can be lowered with the voltage bias, as a platform in which excitons and magnons can instead couple resonantly. Starting from the microscopic exchange interactions between electrons and localized magnetic moments, we demonstrate the linear hybridization of magnons and spin-flip excitons in this regime. As the exciton energy is lowered further, a magnon--exciton Bose--Einstein condensate is formed. We show that this condensate is further modified by an attractive magnon--exciton density--density interaction, which we derive microscopically. We study the condensate's collective modes and demonstrate their hybridization with the magnons, providing an alternative detection mechanism for the formation of exciton condensates.

AI.tldr: A biased ferromagnetic electron-hole bilayer is proposed as a platform for resonant magnon-exciton coupling, enabling magnon spin-flip exciton hybridization and a magnon-exciton Bose-Einstein condensate with detectable collective modes.
AI.motivation: Two-dimensional magnetic semiconductors allow strong magnon-exciton interactions, but the intrinsic energy mismatch between excitons and magnons means interactions typically occur only between exciton density and magnons rather than resonantly. This work aims to overcome this mismatch and achieve resonant coupling.
AI.method: Starting from microscopic exchange interactions between electrons and localized magnetic moments, the authors analyze biased ferromagnetic electron-hole bilayers. The voltage bias lowers the exciton energy gap, allowing resonant coupling. They derive the linear hybridization of magnons and spin-flip excitons, identify a magnon-exciton Bose-Einstein condensate as the exciton energy is further lowered, microscopically derive an attractive magnon-exciton density-density interaction, and study the condensate's collective modes.
AI.result: Resonant linear hybridization of magnons and spin-flip excitons is demonstrated. A magnon-exciton Bose-Einstein condensate forms at lower exciton energy. The condensate is modified by a microscopically derived attractive magnon-exciton density-density interaction. The condensate's collective modes hybridize with magnons.
AI.conclusion: Biased ferromagnetic electron-hole bilayers enable resonant magnon-exciton coupling, magnon-exciton Bose-Einstein condensation, and hybridization of collective modes with magnons, offering an alternative detection mechanism for exciton condensate formation.

title: Haldane-Holstein model at fractional filling: Route to bosonic fractional Chern insulator and quantum anomalous Hall crystal
summary: Electron-phonon coupling is generally expected to suppress band topology, driving a topological band insulator into a trivial phase. Here we show that, using the prototypical Haldane-Holstein model at partial filling of a topological band, strong electron-phonon coupling can instead stabilize topological phases of matter.
