The electron-phonon coupling plays a double role: it generates the longer-range interactions that correlate the carriers and, in the attractive channel, also binds them into bosonic pairs. For spinful electrons, it pairs opposite spins into charge-$2e$ bipolarons that form a bosonic fractional Chern insulator (FCI) at filling $ν=1/2$ with charge-$e$ semionic excitations. Tuning the band topology and the coupling strength maps out a rich phase diagram containing this bosonic FCI, superconductors condensed at the $M$ and $K$ points, and several charge-ordered solids. For spin-polarized electrons, strong coupling instead stabilizes a $C=2$ quantum anomalous Hall crystal (QAHC) at $ν=1/3$. Electron-phonon coupling thus emerges as a route to, rather than an obstruction against, topology in partially filled Chern bands.

AI.tldr: Using the Haldane-Holstein model at partial filling, strong electron-phonon coupling can stabilize topological phases (a bosonic fractional Chern insulator and a quantum anomalous Hall crystal) rather than destroy band topology.
AI.motivation: Electron-phonon coupling is conventionally expected to suppress band topology, driving a topological band insulator into a trivial phase. The authors challenge this assumption by asking whether strong coupling can instead promote topology in partially filled Chern bands.
AI.method: The study employs the prototypical Haldane-Holstein model at partial filling of a topological band. It analyzes the dual role of electron-phonon coupling: generating longer-range interactions that correlate carriers, and, in the attractive channel, binding them into bosonic pairs.
AI.result: For spinful electrons, opposite spins pair into charge-2e bipolarons forming a bosonic fractional Chern insulator (FCI) at filling ν=1/2 with charge-e semionic excitations. Tuning band topology and coupling strength yields a rich phase diagram including the bosonic FCI, superconductors condensed at the M and K points, and several charge-ordered solids. For spin-polarized electrons, strong coupling stabilizes a C=2 quantum anomalous Hall crystal (QAHC) at ν=1/3.
AI.conclusion: Electron-phonon coupling emerges as a route to, rather than an obstruction against, topology in partially filled Chern bands.

title: Binder chemistry sets the interfacial balance constant in CsPbBr$_3$ nanocrystal supercapacitor electrodes
summary: Previous work on lead-free tin halide perovskites showed that the binder instead sets the electrolyte concentration at which capacitance is maximised, following the relationship $100 \times [\mathrm{Li}^+]_{\mathrm{opt}} + \mathrm{PVDF}_{\mathrm{wt}\%} = ξ_{\mathrm{Int}}$ with $ξ_{\mathrm{Int}} = 25 \pm 2.5$, established by varying the loading of a single polymer. Whether $ξ_{\mathrm{Int}}$ is universal or specific to that polymer has not been tested. Here, four binders spanning fluorinated (PVDF), carboxylic (PAA), cellulosic (CMC) and sulfonic (PEDOT:PSS) chemistry are compared on $\mathrm{CsPbBr_3}$ nanocrystal electrodes at four LiTFSI concentrations in acetonitrile, with binder loading fixed at 15 wt% and all other formulation variables held constant. The relationship applies to $\mathrm{CsPbBr_3}$: PVDF at 15 wt% gives an optimum at 0.10--0.15 M and 112 F g$^{-1}$, against 126 F g$^{-1}$ reported for $\mathrm{CsSnCl_3}$ under the same conditions, extending the result to a different B-site cation, halide and crystal system. PVDF and CMC optimise at 0.10 M, giving $ξ_{\mathrm{Int}} = 25$, while PAA and PEDOT:PSS optimise at 0.15 M, giving $ξ_{\mathrm{Int}} = 30$, with maximum values of 188 F g$^{-1}$ for PAA and 146 mF cm$^{-2}$ for PEDOT:PSS. The two binders showing the shift carry ionisable acid groups at high density, indicating that $ξ_{\mathrm{Int}}$ expressed in weight percent requires a binder-specific value. In all four electrodes, $\mathrm{CsPbBr_3}$ converts to $\mathrm{PbBr_2}$ and CsBr during electrochemical characterisation, and the surface lead content of the PEDOT:PSS electrode decreases.

AI.tldr: Four binders (PVDF, PAA, CMC, PEDOT:PSS) at 15 wt% on CsPbBr3 nanocrystal electrodes were tested across four LiTFSI concentrations. The prior relationship linking optimal electrolyte concentration and binder loading generalizes to a new perovskite system and B-site cation, but the constant is binder-specific: PVDF/CMC give ξInt=25 while PAA/PEDOT:PSS (high-density ionisable acid groups) give ξInt=30.
AI.motivation: Prior work established the relation 100×[Li+]opt + PVDF wt% = ξInt (25 ± 2.5) for tin halide perovskites using a single polymer binder, leaving unresolved whether ξInt is universal across binders or specific to PVDF, and whether it extends beyond one B-site cation, halide and crystal system.
AI.method: CsPbBr3 nanocrystal electrodes were formulated with four binders spanning different chemistries—fluorinated (PVDF), carboxylic (PAA), cellulosic (CMC) and sulfonic (PEDOT:PSS)—all fixed at 15 wt% loading with other formulation variables constant. Each was characterised at four LiTFSI concentrations in acetonitrile, with capacitance metrics and post-electrochemical compositional changes (CsPbBr3 conversion to PbBr2 and CsBr, surface lead content) assessed.
AI.result: PVDF at 15 wt% on CsPbBr3 optimises at 0.10–0.15 M with 112 F g−1, versus 126 F g−1 previously reported for CsSnCl3 under identical conditions. PVDF and CMC optimise at 0.10 M (ξInt = 25); PAA and PEDOT:PSS optimise at 0.15 M (ξInt = 30), with maxima of 188 F g−1 for PAA and 146 mF cm−2 for PEDOT:PSS. All four electrodes convert CsPbBr3 to PbBr2 and CsBr during characterisation, and the PEDOT:PSS electrode shows decreased surface lead content.
AI.conclusion: The optimal-concentration/binder-loading relationship extends to a different B-site cation, halide and crystal system, indicating generality of the phenomenon. However, ξInt expressed in weight percent is not universal: binders bearing ionisable acid groups at high density (PAA, PEDOT:PSS) shift the optimum and yield ξInt = 30, so a binder-specific constant is required.

title: Altermagnetism across the BCS-BEC crossover
summary: We study a two-dimensional paired Fermi system in which altermagnetism produces a spin splitting that depends on momentum. The interaction strength is described through the two-body binding energy, so that the chemical potential and pairing gap evolve self-consistently from the weak-coupling Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer (BCS) regime to the strong-coupling Bose-Einstein-condensate (BEC) regime at fixed density. The stability of the uniform paired state is examined by giving the pairs a small center-of-mass momentum and following the resulting change in free energy. We show that at zero temperature, the phase stiffness follows a universal quadratic suppression, $J/J_0 = 1 - (α/α_0)^2$, across the entire fully gapped crossover regime. Deviations from this relation emerge only on the BCS side upon the opening of gapless Bogoliubov pockets, which rapidly reduce the stiffness and can trigger an instability toward finite-momentum pairing. In the BEC regime, this universal quadratic correction corresponds to the altered effective mass of the tightly bound composite bosons. The model therefore provides a simple setting in which to compare altermagnetic pair breaking on the BCS and BEC sides of the crossover.

AI.tldr: A 2D paired Fermi system with momentum-dependent altermagnetic spin splitting is studied across the BCS-BEC crossover; the phase stiffness exhibits a universal quadratic suppression J/J0 = 1 − (α/α0)² in the fully gapped regime, with deviations and possible finite-momentum pairing instability on the BCS side.
AI.motivation: Altermagnetism generates momentum-dependent spin splitting whose effect on pairing and superfluid stiffness across the BCS-BEC crossover is not well understood; the paper seeks a tractable model to compare altermagnetic pair breaking on both sides of the crossover.
AI.method: Two-dimensional paired Fermi system with momentum-dependent altermagnetic spin splitting. Interaction strength is parametrized by two-body binding energy, with chemical potential and pairing gap determined self-consistently at fixed density from weak-coupling BCS to strong-coupling BEC. Uniform paired-state stability is probed by imparting a small center-of-mass momentum to the pairs and tracking the free-energy change.
AI.result: At zero temperature, phase stiffness obeys a universal quadratic suppression J/J0 = 1 − (α/α0)² throughout the fully gapped crossover regime. Deviations appear only on the BCS side when gapless Bogoliubov pockets open, rapidly reducing stiffness and potentially driving an instability toward finite-momentum pairing. In the BEC regime the quadratic correction maps onto the modified effective mass of tightly bound composite bosons.
AI.conclusion: The model offers a simple framework for contrasting altermagnetic pair breaking on the BCS and BEC sides of the crossover, with the universal stiffness suppression as a unifying signature and finite-momentum pairing as a BCS-side instability.

title: Quantum Hall Ferromagnetism in a Cavity Vacuum
summary: We uncover a continuous phase transition in a quantum Hall ferromagnet (QHF) at filling factor $ν=1$, driven by vacuum fluctuations of a cavity. Our analysis starts with a Landau level projection in dipole gauge, where we find the states to be well-represented by a tensor product of the electronic and photonic degrees of freedom. Through analytic spin wave calculations, mean-field theory and density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) simulations, we show that for a spatially antisymmetric cavity field, the uniform QHF state is stable only for weak light-matter coupling and gives way to states of inhomogeneous electron density above a critical coupling. These states involve "flanks" of uniform QHF fluids, separated by a "compact core" of doubly occupied orbitals with the core size being the order parameter, which we dub as "compact-core phases". While the fully spin polarized electronic states are product states, entanglement builds up between the uniform QHF flanks across the compact core in the $S_z=0$ magnetic sector, motivating an ansatz for the compact-core electronic states. The transition boundary is exactly derived for product electronic states in terms of matter and cavity parameters, and numerically confirmed by DMRG. We also study the thin-cylinder limit near the critical point where quantum fluctuations are enhanced, and the many-body excited states in both phases by focusing on the entanglement spectrum degeneracies. Remarkably, the photon number is found to probe the order parameter of the transition, providing a possible experimental signature of the electronic transition and the compact-core states. Our study offers a rare example of a phase of electrons stabilized solely by coupling to the enhanced vacuum fluctuations of a cavity mode.

AI.tldr: A continuous phase transition in a ν=1 quantum Hall ferromagnet is driven purely by cavity vacuum fluctuations, producing "compact-core phases" whose order parameter is the core size and is probed by the photon number.
AI.motivation: The paper explores whether enhanced vacuum fluctuations of a cavity mode can, by themselves, stabilize a distinct electronic phase—an uncommon scenario where light-matter coupling alone (without real photons) reorganizes an interacting electron system.
AI.method: Landau level projection in dipole gauge yielding a tensor-product electronic-photonic description; analytic spin wave calculations; mean-field theory; DMRG simulations; exact derivation of the transition boundary for product electronic states; study of the thin-cylinder limit near criticality; entanglement spectrum degeneracy analysis of many-body excited states.
AI.result: For a spatially antisymmetric cavity field, the uniform QHF state is stable only at weak light-matter coupling and yields to inhomogeneous-density states beyond a critical coupling. These comprise uniform QHF "flanks" separated by a "compact core" of doubly occupied orbitals, with the core size acting as the order parameter. Fully spin-polarized states are product states, while entanglement builds between flanks across the core in the Sz=0 sector. The transition boundary is exactly derived and confirmed by DMRG. Photon number tracks the order parameter, offering an experimental signature.
AI.conclusion: The work presents a rare example of an electronic phase stabilized solely by coupling to enhanced cavity vacuum fluctuations, with the photon number serving as a measurable probe of the transition and of the compact-core states.

title: Beyond binary at submicron dimensions: crossed-ellipse MTJ free layers as multi-state cells for spintronic crossbars
summary: Spintronic crossbars are promising hardware platforms for energy-efficient neuromorphic computing, but conventional magnetic tunnel junctions (MTJs) are binary, limiting the information density and synaptic precision of each crosspoint. Here, MuMax3 micromagnetic simulations are used to investigate how size and aspect ratio control the switching and remanent-state landscape of crossed-ellipse MTJ free layers, with permalloy as the main model system and CoFeB checks for transferability. At fixed 8:1 aspect ratio, shrinking the device from 16 micron x 2 micron to 80 nm x 10 nm lowers the absolute switching current but raises the switching field from about 11 Oe to about 301 Oe and increases the SOT current density. At fixed major axis 1.6 micron, aspect-ratio tuning produces a low-field four-state regime, while lower aspect ratios stabilize additional remanent states with lower switching fields and current densities. A 1.6 micron x 0.8 micron device exhibits twelve accessible remanent plateaus in its angle-resolved planar Hall response, with the resolved state count depending on both aspect ratio and absolute size. Projected MTJ readout gives multiple electrical levels, while minimum-energy-path calculations show that the twelve configurations are not all thermally independent. Independent MuMax+ calculations reproduce the multistate topology and reveal lower-barrier multistep escape pathways between nominally distant states. These results define a geometry-dependent design window for scalable multistate spintronic crossbar cells.

AI.tldr: MuMax3 micromagnetic simulations show that size and aspect ratio of crossed-ellipse MTJ free layers control the number of accessible remanent states, enabling geometry-tuned multistate spintronic crossbar cells, though not all twelve observed states are thermally independent.
AI.motivation: Conventional MTJs are binary, which caps the information density and synaptic precision per crosspoint in spintronic crossbars for neuromorphic computing; a route to multistate operation via geometry is needed.
AI.method: MuMax3 micromagnetic simulations of crossed-ellipse MTJ free layers (permalloy main model system, CoFeB transferability checks), varying size at fixed 8:1 aspect ratio and varying aspect ratio at fixed 1.6 micron major axis; angle-resolved planar Hall response, projected MTJ readout, minimum-energy-path barrier calculations, and independent MuMax+ verification.
AI.result: Shrinking from 16 micron x 2 micron to 80 nm x 10 nm lowers absolute switching current but raises switching field (~11 Oe to ~301 Oe) and SOT current density. Aspect-ratio tuning yields a low-field four-state regime; a 1.6 micron x 0.8 micron device shows twelve remanent plateaus in angle-resolved planar Hall response, with state count depending on aspect ratio and size. Minimum-energy-path calculations indicate these configurations are not all thermally independent; MuMax+ reveals lower-barrier multistep escape pathways.
AI.conclusion: A geometry-dependent design window is defined for scalable multistate spintronic crossbar cells, while thermal independence of the multistates must be accounted for in design.

title: Proximity-induced charge density waves in a moiré heterobilayer
summary: Twisted heterobilayers of two-dimensional materials have emerged as a platform for studying emergent phases of matter. In this work, we investigate charge density waves (CDW) in a twisted NbSe$_2$/MoSe$_2$ bilayer using first-principles calculations. We observe CDW formation in both layers, even though MoSe$_2$ does not feature a CDW in its monolayer form. Moreover, we find that the CDW is highly non-uniform with filled-center, hollow-center and hexagonal CDWs coexisting in the moiré unit cells of both layers. We assess different mechanisms of CDW formation in the MoSe$_2$ layer and conclude that the dominant one is the steric repulsion between Se atoms across the van der Waals gap. The strength of this effect is highly sensitive to the interlayer separation, which explains why the CDW amplitude in the MoSe$_2$ layer depends strongly on the local stacking arrangement. Our work demonstrates that novel broken-symmetry phases can be induced in twisted heterobilayers through proximity effects.

AI.tldr: First-principles study shows twisted NbSe$_2$/MoSe$_2$ heterobilayers host CDWs in both layers, with three coexisting CDW patterns in each moiré cell; the CDW in MoSe$_2$ is driven mainly by interlayer Se–Se steric repulsion, making its amplitude stackingsensitive.
AI.motivation: Twisted 2D heterobilayers are a platform for emergent phases, but the mechanisms by which a non-CDW material can acquire a broken-symmetry phase via proximity to a CDW partner remain unclear. This work aims to understand CDW formation and its origin in a twisted NbSe$_2$/MoSe$_2$ bilayer.
AI.method: First-principles (DFT) calculations of a twisted NbSe$_2$/MoSe$_2$ bilayer, examining CDW formation in both layers, mapping CDW patterns within moiré unit cells, and assessing candidate mechanisms (notably interlayer steric repulsion between Se atoms) and their dependence on interlayer separation and local stacking.
AI.result: CDWs form in both layers, including MoSe$_2$, despite MoSe$_2$ lacking a CDW as a monolayer. The CDW is highly non-uniform, with filled-center, hollow-center, and hexagonal CDW patterns coexisting in the moiré unit cells of both layers. The dominant mechanism for MoSe$_2$ is steric repulsion between Se atoms across the van der Waals gap; its strength is highly sensitive to interlayer separation, explaining the strong stacking dependence of the MoSe$_2$ CDW amplitude.
AI.conclusion: Proximity effects in twisted heterobilayers can induce novel broken-symmetry phases in materials that are not intrinsically unstable, here yielding a stacking-dependent, spatially non-uniform CDW in MoSe$_2$ driven by interlayer steric repulsion.

title: Quantitative control and recording of materials-synthesis processes using an automated experimentation platform
summary: Data-driven materials development requires the collection of large amounts of high-quality materials data. Full autonomy of materials experiments is anticipated, but its technical hurdles are high and its adoption remains limited. In this study, we constructed a simple, easy-to-deploy automated experimentation platform that focuses not on full autonomy but on the reliable automation and quantitative recording of experimental processes. Specifically, commercially available instruments such as robot arms, electric pipettes, web cameras, and an electronic balance are combined, components such as fixtures are fabricated with a 3D printer, and the instruments are operated by control code generated by an AI agent based on a large language model. As a demonstration, we applied the platform to a two-solution mixing experimental system and synthesized ZIF-8, a metal-organic framework. A white suspension phase was observed in the product, and X-ray diffraction measurements confirmed that it was ZIF-8. We also found that its particle size distribution depends strongly on the solution dispensing speed of the electric pipette, which is a parameter that is difficult to control or record in manual operation. This dependence was reproduced in repeated runs, confirming the repeatability of the automated synthesis. This result is a good example showing that the control and recording of process parameters that are rarely quantified in manual work can govern the quality of materials data. All control code, CAD models, and documentation are made publicly available to encourage the spread of laboratory-scale automation of experiments.

AI.tldr: A low-cost, easy-to-deploy automated experimentation platform built from commercial instruments and 3D-printed fixtures, operated by LLM-agent-generated control code, was demonstrated by synthesizing ZIF-8 and revealing that solution dispensing speed governs particle size distribution reproducibly.
AI.motivation: Data-driven materials development requires large amounts of high-quality materials data. While full autonomy of materials experiments is anticipated, its technical hurdles are high and adoption remains limited, so a more practical intermediate approach is needed.
AI.method: The authors constructed a simple automated experimentation platform emphasizing reliable automation and quantitative recording rather than full autonomy. Commercially available instruments (robot arms, electric pipettes, web cameras, electronic balance) were combined with 3D-printed fixtures, and instruments were operated by control code generated by an LLM-based AI agent. The platform was applied to a two-solution mixing system to synthesize the metal-organic framework ZIF-8.
AI.result: A white suspension phase was observed in the product, and X-ray diffraction confirmed ZIF-8 formation. The particle size distribution depended strongly on the solution dispensing speed of the electric pipette, a parameter hard to control or record manually. This dependence was reproduced in repeated runs, confirming repeatability of the automated synthesis.
AI.conclusion: Controlling and recording process parameters that are rarely quantified in manual work can govern materials data quality. All control code, CAD models, and documentation are publicly released to promote laboratory-scale automation of experiments.

title: Thermally stimulated depolarization in hafnium oxide: experiment and numerical simulation
summary: This paper presents an experimental and theoretical study of thermally stimulated depolarization (TSD) in hafnium oxide. Three different models for the probability of trap ionization are considered: the Frenkel effect and two variants of the multiphonon trap ionization mechanism, the multiphonon ionization mechanism of isolated traps at low trap concentrations and phonon-assisted tunneling between neighboring traps at high trap concentrations. The best agreement between the TSD experiment and theory is observed for the multiphonon ionization mechanism of isolated traps. Similar thermal energies of electron and hole traps in HfO2 are obtained ~ 1.3 eV.

AI.tldr: This study combines experiment and theory to investigate thermally stimulated depolarization (TSD) in hafnium oxide, comparing three trap ionization models and identifying multiphonon ionization of isolated traps as the best fit, yielding similar electron and hole trap thermal energies of ~1.3 eV.
AI.motivation: The trap ionization mechanism in HfO2 is not well established; identifying the correct model is essential to accurately describe charge trapping and depolarization behavior.
AI.method: Experimental TSD measurements on hafnium oxide were compared against three theoretical models of trap ionization probability: the Frenkel effect, multiphonon ionization of isolated traps at low trap concentration, and phonon-assisted tunneling between neighboring traps at high trap concentration.
AI.result: The multiphonon ionization mechanism of isolated traps shows the best agreement with the TSD experiment. Comparable thermal energies of approximately 1.3 eV are obtained for both electron and hole traps in HfO2.
AI.conclusion: The multiphonon ionization model of isolated traps best describes TSD in HfO2, and both electron and hole traps exhibit similar thermal energies near 1.3 eV.

title: Demonstrate of High-Performance Top-Gate ALD Crystalline In2O3 Transistor Enabled by Lattice-Matched HfO2 and In2O3 Heterostructure
summary: In this work, we demonstrate high-mobility top-gate (TG) atomic-layer-deposited (ALD) crystalline In2O3 transistors through simultaneous interface and crystallinity engineering. First, a HfO2/In2O3/HfO2 stack is employed, enabling epitaxial-like crystallization of the ultrathin In2O3 channel, because of the lattice matching between monoclinic phase HfO2 and cubic phase In2O3. Second, an oxygen-rich gate insulator process is applied using high-dose O3 precursor and elevated deposition temperature, effectively suppressing oxygen scavenging during gate dielectric deposition, significantly reducing interfacial defect formation. Third, the homogeneous In-O bonding network in crystalline In2O3 exhibits substantially enhanced resistance to oxygen scavenging by source/drain contacts, which significantly improves the immunity to threshold voltage (VTH) roll-off at short channel length compared to amorphous In2O3. As a result, high-performance TG long-channel In2O3 transistors are achieved with a high mobility of 163 cm2/V s and a steep subthreshold slope of 64 mV/dec. High-performance TG short-channel In2O3 transistors with high ION of 1650 μA/μm at VD of 1 V, large on/off ratio over 1010 and VTH of -0.27 V are demonstrated. These results establish lattice-engineered crystalline In2O3 as an effective strategy for high-mobility, aggressively scaled TG oxide transistors suitable for BEOL-compatible applications.

AI.tldr: This work achieves high-mobility top-gate ALD crystalline In2O3 transistors via simultaneous interface and crystallinity engineering, reaching a mobility of 163 cm2/V s and excellent short-channel performance.
AI.motivation: High-mobility, aggressively scaled top-gate oxide transistors are needed for BEOL-compatible applications, but amorphous In2O3 suffers from interfacial defects and threshold voltage roll-off at short channel lengths due to oxygen scavenging.
AI.method: A HfO2/In2O3/HfO2 stack enables epitaxial-like crystallization of the ultrathin In2O3 channel via lattice matching between monoclinic HfO2 and cubic In2O3. An oxygen-rich gate insulator process using high-dose O3 precursor and elevated deposition temperature suppresses oxygen scavenging and reduces interfacial defects. The homogeneous In-O bonding network in crystalline In2O3 resists oxygen scavenging by source/drain contacts.
AI.result: Long-channel TG In2O3 transistors show a mobility of 163 cm2/V s and a subthreshold slope of 64 mV/dec. Short-channel devices exhibit high ION of 1650 μA/μm at VD of 1 V, on/off ratio over 1010, and VTH of -0.27 V.
AI.conclusion: Lattice-engineered crystalline In2O3 is established as an effective strategy for high-mobility, aggressively scaled top-gate oxide transistors suitable for BEOL-compatible applications.

title: A cylindrical sintering method for more realistic grain boundaries in nanocrystalline thin films
summary: Discrepancies between simulated and experimental mechanical properties in molecular dynamics simulations of nanocrystalline metals typically arise from the sample-construction method and the interatomic potential choice. We introduce a cylindrical sintering method to generate nanocrystalline aluminum thin-film samples with wider, more disordered grain boundaries than the usual Voronoi tessellation method, while maintaining deterministic control over grain size, shape, and orientation. Cylindrical sintered samples are benchmarked against hexagonal Voronoi references under identical conditions using both the classical Pascuet15 MEAM and tabGAP machine-learning potentials. Cylindrical sintered samples consistently show lower mechanical properties than hexagonal Voronoi samples due to their wider, more disordered grain boundaries - an effect independent of the choice of potential. Notably, changing the sample geometry and changing the interatomic potential produce comparable, additive, and independent shifts in predicted properties, highlighting that future molecular dynamics studies must hold both variables fixed for meaningful comparisons. Common neighbor and dislocation extraction analyses confirm that deformation is dominated by grain-boundary-mediated plasticity. Uniaxial tensile tests reveal an inverse Hall-Petch relationship for both sample types and both potentials, with mechanical properties decreasing monotonically as grain size reduces from 40.34 to 4.84 nm. The cylindrical sintering method offers a physically realistic, geometrically controlled alternative that bridges idealized Voronoi models and disordered experimental grain-boundary structures.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a cylindrical sintering method for building nanocrystalline Al thin-film samples with wider, more disordered grain boundaries than Voronoi tessellation, showing that sample construction and interatomic potential produce comparable, additive, independent shifts in predicted mechanical properties.
AI.motivation: Discrepancies between simulated and experimental mechanical properties in molecular dynamics studies of nanocrystalline metals commonly stem from the sample-construction method and the choice of interatomic potential. Existing idealized Voronoi models may not capture realistic disordered grain-boundary structures, motivating a geometrically controlled, physically realistic alternative.
AI.method: A cylindrical sintering method is developed to generate nanocrystalline aluminum thin-film samples with wider, more disordered grain boundaries, while retaining deterministic control over grain size, shape, and orientation. Cylindrical sintered samples are benchmarked against hexagonal Voronoi references under identical conditions using the classical Pascuet15 MEAM potential and the tabGAP machine-learning potential. Deformation mechanisms are examined via common neighbor and dislocation extraction analyses, and uniaxial tensile tests are performed across grain sizes from 40.34 to 4.84 nm.
AI.result: Cylindrical sintered samples consistently exhibit lower mechanical properties than hexagonal Voronoi samples due to their wider, more disordered grain boundaries, independent of the potential used. Changing sample geometry and changing the interatomic potential produce comparable, additive, and independent shifts in predicted properties. Deformation is dominated by grain-boundary-mediated plasticity, and an inverse Hall-Petch relationship is observed for both sample types and both potentials, with mechanical properties decreasing monotonically as grain size decreases.
AI.conclusion: The cylindrical sintering method provides a physically realistic, geometrically controlled alternative that bridges idealized Voronoi models and disordered experimental grain-boundary structures. Future molecular dynamics studies must hold both sample-construction method and interatomic potential fixed for meaningful comparisons.

title: Optical properties of As2Se3 from first principles
summary: Crystalline As2Se3 is a promising layered chalcogenide for mid-infrared photonics and optoelectronic applications, yet its fundamental electronic and optical properties remain debated. This paper combines density functional theory with G0W0 quasiparticle corrections and Bethe-Salpeter equation (BSE) calculations to deliver a robust description of its band structure and optical response. The G0W0 results reveal an indirect band gap of 2.31 eV with nearly degenerate direct transitions at Gamma, while the BSE spectra exhibit strong polarization-dependent anisotropy and pronounced excitonic effects. Several bound excitons are identified near the absorption onset, clarifying the role of electron-hole interactions and resolving previous controversies regarding the nature of the optical gap and the contribution of lone-pair states. This work provides a unified and quantitatively accurate picture of As2Se3, reinforcing its potential for next-generation infrared and anisotropic photonic devices.

AI.tldr: DFT with G0W0 and BSE calculations resolve the debated electronic and optical properties of crystalline As2Se3, revealing an indirect gap of 2.31 eV, strong polarization anisotropy, and bound excitons near the absorption onset.
AI.motivation: Crystalline As2Se3 is a promising layered chalcogenide for mid-infrared photonics and optoelectronics, but its fundamental electronic and optical properties remain debated, particularly the nature of the optical gap and the contribution of lone-pair states.
AI.method: The authors combine density functional theory (DFT) with G0W0 quasiparticle corrections and Bethe-Salpeter equation (BSE) calculations to describe the band structure and optical response, including excitonic effects.
AI.result: G0W0 yields an indirect band gap of 2.31 eV with nearly degenerate direct transitions at Gamma. BSE spectra show strong polarization-dependent anisotropy and pronounced excitonic effects, with several bound excitons identified near the absorption onset.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a unified, quantitatively accurate picture of As2Se3, clarifies electron-hole interaction effects, resolves prior controversies on the optical gap and lone-pair states, and reinforces its potential for next-generation infrared and anisotropic photonic devices.

title: From bending to stretching driven peeling of heterogeneous adhesives
summary: We study theoretically the peeling behavior of adhesives. Adopting a fracture mechanics approach, we derive the equation of motion of the adhesion front propagating at the interface between the adhesive and the substrate from which the peel strength is inferred. The originality of our approach lies in the description of the interplay during peeling between the stretching and the bending modes of deformation of the adhesive that is described as a F{\''o}ppl-Von Karman's thin film. Considering first a straight adhesion front, we retrieve the most salient feature of homogeneous adhesives, namely a peeling angle dependent peel strength driven by bending at large angles and by stretching at low angles. We also derive the shape of the adhesive that can be described using a single bending length scale derived from our model. We then investigate the impact of adhesion heterogeneities. We evidence that the deformations of the adhesion front are governed by a non-local interface elasticity the strength of which decreases with the peeling angle. This phenomenon reflects the transition between a stretching dominated peeling at low angle to a bending driven peeling at large angles that is captured in our model. This transition impacts the stability of adhesive fronts that relaxe more slowly from perturbations and gives rise to a stronger toughening effect in presence of a disorder distribution of adhesion energy at low peeling angles. Overall, this study sheds light on the central role played the elastic deformations of adhesives on their peeling behavior. The proposed framework unfolds the complex interplay between the deformation of adhesives and the peeling driving force that may be leveraged to engineer heterogeneous adhesives with enhanced properties. It also provides rich insights on the mechanisms underlying the emergence of non-local elasticity in interface problems.

AI.tldr: Using a fracture mechanics approach, this work derives the peeling equation of motion for adhesives modeled as Föppl–von Kármán thin films, revealing a transition from stretching-dominated peeling at low angles to bending-driven peeling at large angles and showing how this transition governs non-local interface elasticity and adhesion-front stability.
AI.motivation: The peeling behavior of adhesives is central to their performance, yet the interplay between the stretching and bending deformation modes of the adhesive during peeling—and how this interplay controls peel strength, front stability, and response to adhesion heterogeneities—is not fully understood. The authors aim to build a theoretical framework that captures this coupling and explains the mechanisms behind non-local interface elasticity.
AI.method: The authors adopt a fracture mechanics approach to derive the equation of motion of the adhesion front propagating along the adhesive–substrate interface. The adhesive is described as a Föppl–von Kármán thin film, capturing the coupling between stretching and bending deformations. They first analyze a straight adhesion front, then introduce adhesion heterogeneities to study front deformation, non-local interface elasticity, and stability.
AI.result: For a straight adhesion front, the model reproduces the peeling-angle-dependent peel strength of homogeneous adhesives: bending dominates at large angles and stretching at low angles. The adhesive shape is described by a single bending length scale. With adhesion heterogeneities, adhesion-front deformations are governed by a non-local interface elasticity whose strength decreases with peeling angle, reflecting the stretching-to-bending transition. This transition slows front relaxation from perturbations and produces a stronger toughening effect under disordered adhesion energy at low peeling angles.
AI.conclusion: The study highlights the central role of elastic deformations in adhesive peeling behavior. The framework clarifies the complex interplay between adhesive deformation and peeling driving force, offering a basis for engineering heterogeneous adhesives with enhanced properties and providing insights into the emergence of non-local elasticity in interface problems.

title: Gate-tunable magnetic damping in van der Waals Heterostructures
summary: Active control of magnetic damping is a crucial capability for the development of low-power, tunable spintronic devices. In this work, we demonstrate that the intrinsic magnetic damping of 2D materials is highly sensitive to the position of the Fermi level relative to spin-orbit driven anti-crossings, or ``spin hot spots.'' Starting from a minimal multi-band model evaluated via Kamberský's breathing Fermi surface theory, we elucidate the fundamental role that energy gaps and band alignment play in governing magnetic dissipation. We then translate these theoretical insights to van der Waals heterostructures, proposing a concrete mechanism for strongly tunable magnetic damping via electrostatic gating. This concept is validated from first principles via density functional theory calculations on a realistic Fe$_3$GeTe$_2$/graphene heterostructure. Our calculations reveal that an out-of-plane electric field selectively shifts the relevant energy bands, enabling the modulation of the heterostructure's magnetic damping over several orders of magnitude. These findings establish a robust theoretical framework and a promising materials platform for electrically tunable magnetization dynamics.

AI.tldr: Intrinsic magnetic damping in 2D materials is highly sensitive to Fermi-level position relative to spin-orbit anti-crossings ("spin hot spots"); using a minimal multi-band model and DFT on a Fe3GeTe2/graphene heterostructure, the authors predict electrostatic gating can modulate damping by several orders of magnitude.
AI.motivation: Active control of magnetic damping is essential for low-power, tunable spintronic devices, but a microscopic understanding of how to electrically tune intrinsic damping in 2D materials and their heterostructures is lacking.
AI.method: A minimal multi-band model evaluated via Kambersky's breathing Fermi surface theory is used to clarify the role of energy gaps and band alignment, and the concept is validated from first principles with DFT calculations on a realistic Fe3GeTe2/graphene van der Waals heterostructure.
AI.result: Magnetic damping depends strongly on the Fermi level relative to spin-orbit driven anti-crossings, controlled by energy gaps and band alignment. In the Fe3GeTe2/graphene heterostructure, an out-of-plane electric field selectively shifts the relevant bands, enabling damping modulation over several orders of magnitude.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a theoretical framework and a promising materials platform (gated van der Waals heterostructures) for electrically tunable magnetization dynamics and low-power spintronic devices.

title: The Case Against Hall-Petch Hardening in High Entropy Carbide Ceramics
summary: Grain size is often used with the Hall-Petch relationship to justify differences in hardness in ceramic materials. Herein, hardness does not vary systematically with grain-size for fully dense, single-phase (Cr,Mo,Ta,V,W)C1-δ high entropy carbide ceramics for grain sizes that varied by a factor of three. Fully dense, single-phase ceramics with grain sizes from 9.3+/-0.3 to 28.8+/-0.7 microns exhibited a pronounced indentation size effect, with Vickers hardness decreasing from ~28-30 GPa at 0.49 N to ~20-21 GPa at 9.81 N, and Berkovich nanohardness ranging from 26 to 30 GPa at 10 mN. However, at a given load, hardness remained within a narrow range across the grain-size series, and no consistent Hall-Petch dependence was resolved. The lack of grain-size dependence likely indicates that the deformation volume sampled by the indenter was not controlled by grain-boundary interactions; instead, hardness was governed primarily by indentation load and local response of the rock salt carbide matrix.

AI.tldr: Hardness of fully dense, single-phase (Cr,Mo,Ta,V,W)C1-δ high-entropy carbide ceramics is independent of grain size across a threefold variation, with hardness governed by indentation load (indentation size effect) rather than Hall-Petch grain-boundary strengthening.
AI.motivation: Grain size is commonly invoked, via the Hall-Petch relationship, to explain hardness differences in ceramic materials. This study tests whether that assumption holds for high-entropy carbide ceramics, where the role of grain boundaries versus the intrinsic response of the rock salt matrix is unclear.
AI.method: Fully dense, single-phase (Cr,Mo,Ta,V,W)C1-δ high-entropy carbide ceramics were fabricated with grain sizes spanning 9.3 ± 0.3 to 28.8 ± 0.7 μm (a threefold range). Vickers hardness was measured over loads from 0.49 N to 9.81 N, and Berkovich nanohardness was measured at 10 mN, allowing hardness to be assessed both as a function of grain size at fixed load and as a function of load.
AI.result: A pronounced indentation size effect was observed: Vickers hardness decreased from ~28–30 GPa at 0.49 N to ~20–21 GPa at 9.81 N, and Berkovich nanohardness ranged from 26 to 30 GPa at 10 mN. At any given load, hardness varied only within a narrow range across the grain-size series, with no consistent Hall-Petch dependence resolved.
AI.conclusion: The absence of grain-size dependence indicates that the deformation volume sampled by the indenter was not controlled by grain-boundary interactions. Instead, hardness is governed primarily by indentation load and the local response of the rock salt carbide matrix, cautioning against using the Hall-Petch relationship to justify hardness differences in these high-entropy carbide ceramics.

title: Twin Domains in Van der Waals Quaternary Oxides
summary: Optical anisotropy is the basis for many intriguing phenomena in van der Waals materials, including hyperbolic polaritons and extreme birefringence. Stacking and twisting van der Waals materials along the out-of-plane direction emerged as a powerful route to tailor this anisotropy, but designing lateral interfaces remains a challenge. Here, twin domains are reported in the van der Waals quaternary oxides MgTeMoO$_6$, MnTeMoO$_6$, ZnTeMoO$_6$, and CoTeMoO$_6$ - materials that possess strong in-plane optical anisotropy and second-order nonlinearity. The domains naturally form in their orthorhombic crystal structure and extend over hundreds of micrometers. It is proposed that this stability is achieved by the domain wall acting as a diagonal mirror plane in the crystal structure, parallel to the (1-10) or (110) crystal planes, resulting in nearly opposite birefringence between domains. This hypothesis is experimentally confirmed by determining the angle between the crystal axes of neighboring domains using polarization-resolved optical microscopy, infrared-visible sum-frequency generation microscopy, and transmission electron microscopy. The latter further allowed an estimate of the domain wall thickness. Overall, the observation of twin domains with orthogonal optical anisotropy opens new routes to use van der Waals quaternary oxides for birefringent waveguiding, polariton steering, and frequency conversion applications.

AI.tldr: Twin domains with orthogonal in-plane optical anisotropy, extending over hundreds of micrometers, form naturally in orthorhombic van der Waals quaternary oxides MgTeMoO6, MnTeMoO6, ZnTeMoO6, and CoTeMoO6, with the domain wall acting as a diagonal mirror plane.
AI.motivation: Optical anisotropy underpins phenomena such as hyperbolic polaritons and extreme birefringence in van der Waals materials. While stacking and twisting along the out-of-plane direction enables tailoring of this anisotropy, designing lateral interfaces remains challenging. This work addresses the need for lateral anisotropy engineering by identifying and characterizing natural twin domains in van der Waals quaternary oxides.
AI.method: The authors investigate twin domains in orthorhombic van der Waals quaternary oxides MgTeMoO6, MnTeMoO6, ZnTeMoO6, and CoTeMoO6, which exhibit strong in-plane optical anisotropy and second-order nonlinearity. They propose that the domain wall acts as a diagonal mirror plane parallel to the (1-10) or (110) crystal planes, yielding nearly opposite birefringence between domains. The hypothesis is tested experimentally by determining the angle between crystal axes of neighboring domains using polarization-resolved optical microscopy, infrared-visible sum-frequency generation microscopy, and transmission electron microscopy, the latter also providing an estimate of domain wall thickness.
AI.result: Twin domains form naturally in the orthorhombic crystal structure and extend over hundreds of micrometers. The measured orientation relationship between neighboring domains confirms the proposed diagonal mirror-plane domain wall, with nearly opposite birefringence between domains, and the domain wall thickness is estimated from transmission electron microscopy.
AI.conclusion: The observation of twin domains with orthogonal optical anisotropy in van der Waals quaternary oxides opens new routes for birefringent waveguiding, polariton steering, and frequency conversion applications, establishing lateral interface design as a viable approach to tailoring optical anisotropy.

title: An Open-Source Hardware and Software Toolkit to Enable Agentic RHEED-Guided Thin-Film Synthesis
summary: Reflection high-energy electron diffraction (RHEED) provides rich information about evolving surfaces during thin-film growth, but non-automated, operator-dependent alignment and fragmented analysis workflows limit its potential in fully autonomous synthesis. Here, we present an open-source hardware and software toolkit that makes RHEED control and quantitative analysis accessible to operators and artificial intelligence (AI) agents. Demonstrated on a pulsed laser deposition system, the toolkit provides programmable electron-optics control, automated beam alignment and rocking-curve acquisition, and a training-free method for crystallographic azimuthal alignment. The auto RHEED application extracts structural and growth-related observables through shared graphical and programmatic interfaces, including a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server. An agent-driven demonstration shows how natural-language requests can guide the selection, configuration, and execution of quantitative analyses. An extensible adapter interface streamlines the incorporation of community-developed methods for AI analysis and RHEED simulation as they emerge, supported by Markdown implementation guides designed for AI coding agents. These capabilities support complementary descriptions of surface evolution through physical measurements and learned image representations while providing a practical route for incorporating new computational methods. Together, these tools reduce barriers to automated and agentic RHEED measurements and establish a foundation for future agentic control of thin-film synthesis guided by the evolving surface.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an open-source hardware and software toolkit that automates RHEED control, beam alignment, and quantitative analysis, exposing these capabilities to both human operators and AI agents via graphical, programmatic, and MCP interfaces to enable more autonomous thin-film synthesis.
AI.motivation: RHEED offers rich information about evolving surfaces during thin-film growth, but operator-dependent manual alignment and fragmented, non-automated analysis workflows hinder its use in fully autonomous synthesis. There is a need to make RHEED control and analysis accessible to both operators and AI agents.
AI.method: The authors developed an open-source hardware and software toolkit demonstrated on a pulsed laser deposition system. It provides programmable electron-optics control, automated beam alignment, automated rocking-curve acquisition, and a training-free method for crystallographic azimuthal alignment. An auto RHEED application extracts structural and growth-related observables through shared graphical and programmatic interfaces, including a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server. An extensible adapter interface, supported by Markdown implementation guides for AI coding agents, allows incorporation of community-developed methods for AI analysis and RHEED simulation.
AI.result: The toolkit enables natural-language agent-driven selection, configuration, and execution of quantitative analyses, and supports complementary descriptions of surface evolution through both physical measurements and learned image representations while providing a practical route to add new computational methods.
AI.conclusion: These tools lower the barriers to automated and agentic RHEED measurements and establish a foundation for future agentic control of thin-film synthesis guided by the evolving surface.

title: Disorder-driven transport in ZrN thin films grown by ion-beam-assisted sputtering
summary: We investigate the structural and electronic transport properties of zirconium nitride (ZrN) thin films grown by dc ion-beam assisted sputtering (IBAS) as a function of nitrogen partial pressure, sputtering power and deposition temperature. Variation of growth conditions enables controlled tuning from disordered metallic and superconducting behavior to insulating transport. Increasing nitrogen flow drives an increase in sheet resistance, suppression of superconducting transition temperature, and non-metallic conduction. XRD shows no measurable change in long range crystallinity or order. In the insulating regime, low-temperature transport is well described by 3D Mott variable-range hopping (VRH), with the characteristic temperature $T_0$ increasing monotonically with sheet resistance over four orders of magnitude. Despite this strong correlation between $T_0$ and disorder, $T_c$ exhibits no systematic dependence on $T_0$, indicating a decoupling between localization physics and the superconducting energy scale. Magnetotransport measurements are not well described by the standard BCS model nor the dirty type-II Werthamer-Helfand-Hohenberg model. The phase boundary is instead captured by a free-exponent power law, $μ_0 H_{c2}(T) = μ_0 H_{c2}(0)[1 - (T/T_c)^{n}]$ with $n \approx 3.47$, and extrapolates to $μ_0 H_{c2}(0) \approx 6.4$ T. The films have an extracted coherence length of 7 nm. These results establish IBAS-grown ZrN as a broadly tunable platform for investigating disorder-driven transport and the crossover between metallic conduction, electronic localization, and superconductivity.

AI.tldr: IBAS-grown ZrN thin films are tuned from superconducting-metallic to insulating regimes via growth conditions; transport follows 3D Mott VRH, and Tc decouples from localization strength, with a non-BCS upper critical field power law (n ≈ 3.47, Hc2(0) ≈ 6.4 T).
AI.motivation: Establish ZrN thin films grown by dc ion-beam assisted sputtering as a tunable material platform to study the interplay between metallic conduction, disorder-induced electronic localization, and superconductivity, and to test whether superconducting and localization energy scales are coupled.
AI.method: ZrN thin films deposited by dc ion-beam assisted sputtering (IBAS), with nitrogen partial pressure, sputtering power, and deposition temperature varied to tune disorder. Structural characterization by XRD; electronic transport including sheet resistance, superconducting transition temperature, magnetotransport (Hc2(T)), and low-temperature conduction analyzed against 3D Mott variable-range hopping (VRH).
AI.result: Increasing nitrogen flow raises sheet resistance, suppresses Tc, and induces non-metallic conduction, while XRD shows no measurable change in long-range crystallinity or order. Insulating transport is well described by 3D Mott VRH with T0 increasing monotonically with sheet resistance over four orders of magnitude. Tc shows no systematic dependence on T0, indicating decoupling of localization physics from the superconducting energy scale. Magnetotransport deviates from both standard BCS and dirty type-II Werthamer-Helfand-Hohenberg models; the phase boundary follows a free-exponent power law with n ≈ 3.47, extrapolating to μ0Hc2(0) ≈ 6.4 T. Extracted coherence length ≈ 7 nm.
AI.conclusion: IBAS-grown ZrN is a broadly tunable platform for investigating disorder-driven transport and the crossover between metallic conduction, electronic localization, and superconductivity, with localization strength decoupled from the superconducting energy scale.

title: The Propagating Nature of Single- and Multimagnons in LaCrO$_3$
summary: The dispersion of an excitation is commonly used to infer its microscopic character: dispersive modes are associated with propagation, whereas nondispersive features are often interpreted as localized. This distinction becomes less straightforward for composite excitations, whose spectral maxima can remain nearly dispersionless even when they are built from propagating quasiparticles. Here we use momentum- and temperature-dependent resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS) to reveal the origin of multimagnon excitations in antiferromagnetic LaCrO$_3$. Whereas the single magnon disperses strongly, the two- and three-magnon features remain nearly flat. On approaching the Neel temperature, thermal population of the magnon band produces an anti-Stokes branch and opens an additional three-magnon channel involving the creation of two magnons and annihilation of one. Its energy and momentum dependence are reproduced by a thermally weighted multimagnon joint density of states calculations. These results establish thermal population as a means of exposing the propagating constituents hidden within nondispersive composite excitations, and position RIXS as a probe of multimagnon dynamics and, ultimately, magnon-magnon interactions.

AI.tldr: Momentum- and temperature-dependent RIXS on antiferromagnetic LaCrO3 shows that two- and three-magnon excitations stay nearly dispersionless despite being built from strongly dispersive single magnons. Thermal magnon population near the Neel temperature opens an anti-Stokes branch and a three-magnon channel, explained by a thermally weighted multimagnon joint density of states.
AI.motivation: Dispersion is conventionally used to classify excitations: dispersive features imply propagation, while nondispersive features are read as localized. This criterion fails for composite excitations, whose spectral maxima can appear nearly flat even when their constituents propagate. The paper aims to resolve the microscopic origin of such nondispersive composite features, using multimagnon excitations in an antiferromagnet as the test case.
AI.method: Momentum- and temperature-dependent resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS) measurements on antiferromagnetic LaCrO3, tracking the single-, two-, and three-magnon features and their evolution with momentum and temperature up to the Neel temperature. Results are compared with a thermally weighted multimagnon joint density of states calculation.
AI.result: The single magnon disperses strongly, whereas the two- and three-magnon features remain nearly flat. Approaching the Neel temperature, thermal population of the magnon band produces an anti-Stokes branch and activates an additional three-magnon channel involving creation of two magnons and annihilation of one. The energy and momentum dependence of these features is reproduced by the thermally weighted multimagnon joint density of states calculation.
AI.conclusion: Thermal magnon population provides a way to expose the propagating constituents hidden inside nondispersive composite excitations. The work establishes RIXS as a probe of multimagnon dynamics and, ultimately, of magnon-magnon interactions.
